3.11 Execution

-- 96 of 613 --

Decision-making determines what should be done.
Execution determines whether that decision successfully becomes
football behaviour.
Within the DPF framework, Execution is the process through which
cognitive intention is translated into observable action within the
dynamic constraints of the game.
Execution is therefore not an isolated technical event.
It is the physical expression of an already completed cognitive process.
Every pass, movement, interception, acceleration, or positional
adjustment represents the visible outcome of numerous invisible
cognitive operations that preceded it.
Execution as Behavioural Expression
Within DPF, execution is understood as the expression of behaviour
rather than the performance of isolated techniques.
Technique provides the means.
Behaviour provides the purpose.
A technically perfect pass that contradicts the collective objective
represents poor execution despite flawless mechanics.
Conversely, a technically imperfect action may still represent effective
execution if it successfully achieves the intended tactical behaviour
under demanding conditions.
Execution should therefore always be evaluated in relation to its
behavioural objective rather than its aesthetic quality.
Execution Under Environmental Constraints

-- 97 of 613 --

Football never allows ideal execution.
Every action is performed under continuously changing constraints.
Time pressure.
Opposition pressure.
Physical fatigue.
Limited space.
Uncertainty.
Collective movement.
Execution therefore represents the player's ability to express intelligent
behaviour despite environmental instability.
The objective is not technical perfection.
The objective is functional effectiveness.
Within DPF, successful execution is defined by its contribution to the
evolving System State, not by technical appearance alone.
Synchronised Execution

-- 98 of 613 --

Football is a collective activity.
Consequently, execution rarely occurs in isolation.
Individual actions constantly interact with the simultaneous actions of
teammates and opponents.
The quality of execution therefore depends not only upon individual
ability but also upon collective synchronisation.
A perfectly timed movement may lose its value if surrounding players
fail to adapt accordingly.
Likewise, an ordinary technical action may become decisive when
performed in harmony with collective behaviour.
Execution is therefore both individual and systemic.
Execution and System Continuity
Within DPF, the ultimate criterion of execution is its contribution to
System Continuity.
Every executed behaviour should strengthen, preserve, or restore the
organisation of the collective system.
Successful execution is therefore measured not only by the immediate
outcome of the action but also by its influence on the team's ability to
sustain coordinated football behaviour during subsequent moments of
play.
Execution is never isolated from what follows.
Every action reshapes the environment and creates the starting point
for the next cognitive cycle.

3.13 Intuition

-- 104 of 613 --

Football often appears to reward instinctive behaviour.
Elite players seem to react without hesitation, occupy spaces before they
become available, intercept passes before they are played, and produce
solutions that appear almost effortless.
To observers, these behaviours are frequently described as intuition.
Within the DPF framework, however, intuition is not regarded as an innate
gift or an inexplicable talent.
It is the natural outcome of a highly developed cognitive architecture.
Intuition emerges when years of accumulated System Knowledge, refined
Mental Models, repeated Pattern Recognition, accurate Anticipation, and
continuous Learning become so deeply integrated that intelligent behaviour
can occur with minimal conscious effort.
Intuition is therefore expertise operating automatically.
Intuition Is Compressed Experience
Elite players do not consciously analyse every football situation.
The speed of the game simply does not allow it.
Instead, previous learning has compressed thousands of experiences into
highly efficient cognitive structures.
These structures allow players to interpret situations almost immediately.
What appears externally as instinct is internally the rapid activation of
knowledge acquired through countless previous interactions with the game.
Within DPF, intuition is therefore understood as compressed experience
rather than unconscious guessing.

This speed does not originate from bypassing cognition.

Because knowledge has been organised, Mental Models refined,

processes occur almost simultaneously.
Decision-making therefore becomes both faster and more reliable.
The player appears to react instantly because the necessary
understanding has already been constructed before conscious
deliberation becomes necessary.
Intuition Preserves System Continuity
Within DPF, intuition serves a collective purpose.
Its value lies not in producing spectacular individual actions but in
enabling intelligent behaviour under conditions of extreme uncertainty
and limited time.
Highly intuitive players preserve System Continuity because they
consistently generate behaviours that maintain collective organisation
before instability becomes visible.
Their actions appear effortless not because football has become easier,
but because their understanding has become deeper.

Intuition cannot be taught directly.
It cannot be explained through lectures or memorised through tactical
diagrams.
Instead, it emerges gradually through repeated interaction with
meaningful football problems.
Every training activity should therefore contribute to the continuous
refinement of the player's cognitive architecture.
The objective is not to teach intuitive actions.
The objective is to create the conditions from which intuition naturally
emerges.
Within DPF, intuition is developed through understanding rather than
repetition alone.

-- 107 of 613 --

The cognitive architecture presented throughout this chapter should
not be understood as a rigid sequence of isolated stages.
It represents a continuously evolving system in which each process
strengthens and supports the others.

Mental Models guide Attention.
Attention directs Scanning.
Scanning provides information for Perception.
Perception enables Pattern Recognition.

Anticipation improves Decision Making.

Execution generates Feedback.
Feedback strengthens Learning.

The cycle therefore never truly ends.
Each completed interaction with the game enriches the player's
cognitive architecture, allowing future behaviour to become
increasingly intelligent, adaptive, and efficient.
Within DPF, football intelligence is not a single ability.
It is the emergent property of an integrated cognitive system operating
in continuous interaction with a dynamic football environment.

Chapter III Closing Reflection

-- 110 of 613 --

Football intelligence is often mistaken for talent.
Within the DPF framework, it is understood differently.
Intelligent football behaviour does not emerge from isolated abilities,
but from the continuous interaction of knowledge, perception, learning,
and adaptation within a dynamic environment.
The objective of coaching is therefore not simply to improve technique
or tactical understanding.
It is to develop the cognitive architecture that enables players to sustain
intelligent behaviour under constantly changing conditions.
As this architecture matures, behaviour becomes progressively faster,
more accurate, more adaptable, and increasingly capable of preserving
System Continuity.
Ultimately, the highest level of football performance is not achieved
when players think more.

4.1 Behaviour as the Expression of Cognition
Football behaviour is often evaluated through visible actions.
A pass.
A run.
A tackle.
A movement.
However, visible actions alone provide only a partial understanding of
performance.
Within the DPF framework, every observable football action represents
the external expression of an internal cognitive process.
Behaviour therefore begins long before movement occurs.
It begins with understanding.
Every behaviour reflects how the player has interpreted the current
System State, recognised relevant relationships, anticipated future
developments, and selected an appropriate response.
The visible movement is merely the final manifestation of this invisible
cognitive sequence.
For this reason, behaviour should never be analysed independently of
cognition.

-- 116 of 613 --

Understanding behaviour requires understanding the thinking that
produced it.
Behaviour Is Purposeful
Within DPF, behaviour is always directed toward a purpose.
Players do not move simply because space exists.
They move to influence relationships.
They do not pass merely to transfer possession.
They pass to achieve a tactical objective.
Every behaviour should therefore be understood according to the
function it performs within the collective system rather than the
physical action through which it is expressed.
A single movement may simultaneously create space, attract pressure,
and generate numerical superiority.
Likewise, identical technical actions may represent entirely different
behaviours depending on their tactical intention.
Behaviour is therefore defined by purpose rather than appearance.
Behaviour Shapes the System
Football is a dynamic network of interacting behaviours.
Every individual action influences teammates, opponents, available
space, and subsequent possibilities.
Consequently, behaviour cannot be understood as an isolated event.
Each behaviour contributes to the continuous evolution of the collective
system.

-- 117 of 613 --

Within DPF, intelligent behaviour strengthens organisation, creates
functional relationships, and preserves the continuity of collective play.
Poor behaviour disrupts these relationships, increases uncertainty, and
weakens the system regardless of technical quality.
The quality of football behaviour should therefore be evaluated
according to its systemic consequences rather than its isolated success.

4.2 Behavioural Principles
If behaviour represents the observable expression of cognition, then
intelligent football requires principles capable of guiding behaviour
under constantly changing conditions.
Within the DPF framework, these principles are referred to as
Behavioural Principles.
Behavioural Principles are the fundamental rules that govern football
behaviour regardless of the specific tactical situation.
Rather than prescribing fixed movements or predetermined solutions,
they provide players with a stable framework for generating adaptive
behaviours that remain consistent with the collective identity of the
team.
For this reason, Behavioural Principles should never be understood as
rigid instructions.
They function as behavioural constraints that preserve coherence while
allowing continuous adaptation.
Principles Rather Than Instructions
Football presents an infinite variety of situations.
No tactical manual can prescribe a unique solution for every possible
event.
Consequently, intelligent football cannot depend upon memorising
actions.
Instead, players require principles capable of guiding behaviour across
continuously changing environments.
Within DPF, principles answer the question:

-- 119 of 613 --

"How should I behave?"
They do not answer:
"What exact action should I perform?"
This distinction is fundamental.
Actions vary.
Principles endure.
Adaptive Behaviour
Because football is dynamic, intelligent behaviour must remain
adaptable.
Behavioural Principles therefore provide direction without restricting
flexibility.
Different players may express the same principle through different
technical actions.
Different situations may require different behaviours while pursuing the
same collective objective.
Adaptability is therefore not the absence of structure.
It is the intelligent application of stable principles under unstable
conditions.

A technically successful action that weakens collective organisation

Behaviour is always evaluated according to its contribution to the

commands.
They are the conditions from which intelligent football naturally
emerges.
This perspective shifts coaching away from controlling every action
toward designing environments in which desirable behaviours become
the most logical response.

4.3 Individual Behaviour
Every collective football system ultimately depends upon the quality of
individual behaviour.
Regardless of tactical organisation, collective performance emerges
through the continuous interaction of individual actions performed by
each player within the evolving environment.
Within the DPF framework, Individual Behaviour represents the
intelligent behavioural expression of a player operating in accordance
with the principles of the collective system.
Individual behaviour is therefore never independent.
Every action performed by a player simultaneously influences
teammates, opponents, available space, and the future evolution of the
System State.
The player should consequently be understood not as an isolated
performer, but as an active component of a dynamic collective network.
Individual Behaviour Is Relational
Football behaviour should never be interpreted solely through the
actions of an individual.
Every movement derives its tactical value from its relationship with
other components of the system.
A forward's movement creates space for a midfielder.
A defender's positioning protects the collective structure.
A supporting run increases passing possibilities.
Within DPF, behaviour is therefore fundamentally relational.

-- 123 of 613 --

Players continuously adjust their actions according to the evolving
relationships surrounding them rather than according to predetermined
movement patterns.
No behaviour possesses intrinsic value.
Its value emerges from the relationships it creates or preserves.
Individual Responsibility Within the System
Every player possesses individual responsibility toward the collective
system.
This responsibility extends beyond technical execution or positional
discipline.
Players must continuously evaluate how their behaviour influences:
 Collective organisation.
 Numerical relationships.
 Functional space.
 Available passing networks.
 Defensive stability.
 Attacking progression.
 Future behavioural possibilities.
Individual responsibility therefore consists of continuously selecting
behaviours that strengthen rather than weaken the collective structure.
Within DPF, responsibility is measured through contribution to the
system rather than individual statistics.

Within DPF, players are not simply participants in the game.
They are continuous designers of the evolving System State.

4.4 Unit Behaviour
Football is neither purely individual nor entirely collective.
Between the behaviour of a single player and the behaviour of the
entire team exists an intermediate level of organisation.
Within the DPF framework, this level is referred to as Unit Behaviour.
A unit is a functional group of players whose behaviours are
continuously coordinated in pursuit of a shared tactical objective.
These units may be permanent, such as the defensive line or midfield
unit, or temporary, emerging dynamically according to the evolving
System State.
Unit Behaviour therefore represents the first level at which individual
intelligence becomes coordinated collective behaviour.
Behaviour Through Coordination
The effectiveness of a unit does not depend upon the quality of its
individual members alone.
Its effectiveness emerges from the quality of coordination between
them.
Players continuously adjust their positioning, timing, spacing,
communication, and movement according to the behaviour of
surrounding teammates.
Within DPF, intelligent Unit Behaviour is characterised by
synchronisation rather than simultaneous action.
Players do not perform identical behaviours.
They perform complementary behaviours.

-- 127 of 613 --

Functional Relationships
Every unit operates through functional relationships rather than fixed
positional structures.
The role of each player constantly adapts according to:
 The current System State.
 The collective objective.
 The behaviour of teammates.
 The behaviour of opponents.
 The availability of space.
 Numerical relationships.
Consequently, Unit Behaviour remains dynamic even when the overall
tactical structure appears stable.
Its organisation emerges through interaction rather than rigid
positioning.
Shared Understanding
Successful Unit Behaviour depends upon shared understanding.
Players within the same unit develop common expectations regarding
movement, support, pressure, protection, and positional balance.
This shared understanding dramatically reduces the need for explicit
communication.
Behaviours become coordinated because every player interprets the
situation through the same behavioural principles.
Within DPF, synchronisation emerges from shared cognition rather than
constant instruction.

-- 128 of 613 --

Football constantly disrupts organisation.
Opponents rotate.
Space changes.
Transitions occur.
Numerical relationships evolve.
An effective unit continuously reorganises itself without losing its
functional identity.
Players exchange responsibilities.
Cover one another.
Compress or expand collectively.
Adjust distances.
Maintain balance.
Adaptation therefore becomes a property of the unit rather than the
responsibility of isolated individuals.

deteriorates.
For this reason, coaches should develop units as adaptive systems
rather than collections of independent players.
The objective is not simply to improve cooperation.
It is to create functional groups capable of preserving System
Continuity under constantly changing tactical conditions.

4.5 Collective Behaviour
Football ultimately transcends the actions of individual players and
functional units.
Its highest level of organisation emerges when the entire team behaves
as a single adaptive system.
Within the DPF framework, Collective Behaviour refers to the
coordinated interaction of all players operating according to shared
behavioural principles in pursuit of a common tactical objective.
Collective Behaviour is therefore not the sum of individual
performances.
It is an emergent property arising from the continuous interaction of
intelligent individuals and synchronised units.
The team behaves as one because every component continuously
adapts to every other component.

-- 131 of 613 --

The Team as a Dynamic System
Within DPF, the football team should not be understood as eleven
independent players occupying positions on the pitch.
Instead, it should be understood as a dynamic network of constantly
evolving relationships.
Every behavioural adjustment influences the entire system.
A defender stepping forward changes midfield behaviour.
Midfield movement reshapes attacking possibilities.
Attacking pressure influences defensive organisation.
No behaviour remains local.
Every action propagates throughout the collective system.
The team therefore behaves as a living network rather than a static
formation.
Shared Behavioural Identity
Collective Behaviour depends upon a common behavioural identity.
Every player may perform different actions.
However, those actions are guided by the same principles.
This shared behavioural identity enables consistency despite continuous
variation in football situations.
The collective therefore remains recognisable even though no two
matches are ever identical.
Within DPF, identity emerges from stable principles rather than
repetitive tactical patterns.

4.6 Behaviour Synchronisation
Collective organisation does not emerge solely because players
understand the same principles.
It emerges because their behaviours remain continuously synchronised
across time, space, and changing tactical conditions.
Within the DPF framework, Behaviour Synchronisation is the
continuous alignment of individual and collective behaviours to
preserve functional organisation throughout the evolving System State.
Synchronisation therefore extends beyond simultaneous movement.
It represents the continuous coordination of intentions, timing,
positioning, and behavioural responses among all components of the
collective system.
Synchronisation Beyond Movement
Football synchronisation should not be understood as players moving
together mechanically.
True synchronisation occurs when players continuously interpret
situations through the same behavioural principles while expressing
different but complementary behaviours.
One player presses.
Another provides cover.
A third blocks passing lanes.
A fourth secures defensive balance.
Although every behaviour differs, all behaviours contribute to the same
collective objective.
Synchronisation therefore reflects unity of purpose rather than
uniformity of action.

-- 135 of 613 --

Synchronisation Across Time
Timing is one of the defining characteristics of elite football behaviour.
The value of any action depends not only upon what is performed, but
also upon when it is performed.
An intelligent press initiated too early may isolate teammates.
A supporting movement performed too late may eliminate passing
options.
Within DPF, synchronisation requires players to coordinate behaviours
across continuously evolving moments rather than isolated events.
Collective intelligence therefore depends upon shared timing as much
as shared understanding.
Synchronisation Across Space
Football organisation is also spatial.
Distances between players continuously expand and contract according
to the evolving System State.
Synchronisation ensures that these spatial relationships remain
functionally effective.
When one player moves forward, surrounding players continuously
reorganise.
When the team compresses defensively, every unit adjusts collectively.
Space is therefore regulated through coordinated behavioural
adaptation rather than fixed positioning.

Teams move together because they understand together.

Behaviour Synchronisation represents one of the primary mechanisms

Continuous coordination prevents local behavioural errors from

Small adjustments made simultaneously by multiple players maintain
collective balance despite constant environmental change.
Elite teams therefore appear organised not because mistakes never

Synchronisation transforms individual adaptation into collective

4.7 Adaptive Behaviour
Football is characterised by continuous uncertainty.
Opponents change their organisation.
Space constantly evolves.
Numerical relationships fluctuate.
Transitions emerge unexpectedly.
No tactical situation remains stable for long.
Within the DPF framework, Adaptive Behaviour is the continuous ability of
players and teams to modify behaviour intelligently while preserving the
collective identity of the system.
Adaptation therefore does not represent a departure from the Game Model.
It represents the mechanism through which the Game Model remains
functional under changing conditions.
Adaptation Is Not Improvisation
Adaptive Behaviour should never be confused with unrestricted
freedom.
Improvisation often abandons collective structure in pursuit of
immediate solutions.
Adaptation, by contrast, preserves the principles of the system while
modifying behavioural expression according to contextual demands.
Players remain flexible.
The system remains coherent.
Within DPF, adaptation is disciplined rather than spontaneous.
It allows intelligent variation without sacrificing collective identity.

The more intelligently a system learns, the more intelligently it adapts.

4.8 System Continuity
Throughout this chapter, behaviour has been examined from multiple
perspectives.
Individual Behaviour.
Unit Behaviour.
Collective Behaviour.
Behaviour Synchronisation.
Adaptive Behaviour.
Although each concept contributes uniquely to football performance,
none represents the ultimate objective of the DPF framework.
Their common purpose is the preservation of System Continuity.
Within DPF, System Continuity is defined as the sustained ability of the
football system to maintain its functional organisation, behavioural
coherence, and collective effectiveness despite continuous
environmental change.
It represents the highest behavioural objective of the game.

-- 143 of 613 --

Continuity Rather Than Stability
System Continuity should not be confused with static stability.
Football is inherently dynamic.
Players move.
Opponents adapt.
Space evolves.
Transitions occur.
Uncertainty constantly emerges.
For this reason, continuity does not require the system to remain
unchanged.
Instead, it requires the system to remain functional while continuously
changing.
Within DPF, continuity is preserved through intelligent adaptation
rather than resistance to change.

-- 144 of 613 --

Every Behaviour Influences Continuity
Every behaviour performed by an individual player influences the future state of
the collective system.
A supporting movement.
A defensive cover.
A pressing action.
A delayed pass.
A body orientation adjustment.
None of these behaviours should be evaluated independently.
Each either strengthens or weakens the continuity of the collective organisation.
Within DPF, behaviour is therefore always assessed according to its systemic
consequences rather than its isolated outcome.
Continuity as Collective Intelligence
Elite football teams rarely maintain perfect organisation.
Instead, they demonstrate an exceptional ability to reorganise rapidly whenever
disruption occurs.
This capacity reflects collective intelligence rather than tactical rigidity.
Players continuously detect instability.
Anticipate its consequences.
Coordinate adaptive behaviours.
Restore functional relationships.
The system therefore survives because intelligent behaviours continuously
regenerate organisation.
System Continuity is not the absence of disruption.
It is the ability to recover before disruption becomes collapse.

Disorder does not.

Without shared principles, football becomes dependent upon individual

Individual quality may occasionally compensate for organisational

They reduce ambiguity.
They improve coordination.
They accelerate decision-making.
Most importantly, they enable every player to contribute toward the
preservation of System Continuity.
Within DPF, principles are therefore not tactical preferences.
They are the operating logic of the entire football system.

6.2 The Hierarchy of Playing Principles
Introduction
Not all Playing Principles operate at the same level of decision-making.
Some govern the team's overall identity.
Others organise behaviour within specific phases of play.
Some influence collective organisation.
Others guide individual actions.
For this reason, Playing Principles should not be understood as an
unordered list.
Within the DPF framework, they form a structured hierarchy in which
every level supports the one below it.
This hierarchy ensures that football behaviour remains coherent across
every situation while allowing sufficient flexibility for intelligent
adaptation.
Level 1 | Universal Principles
Universal Principles represent the highest level of the behavioural
hierarchy.
They remain valid regardless of the phase of play, tactical context, or
field location.
These principles define the identity of the Game Model itself.
Every other principle derives from them.

-- 188 of 613 --

Level 2 | Phase Principles
The demands of football differ according to the phase of play.
Attacking 189rganization requires different behavioural priorities from
defensive 189rganization.

Phase Principles therefore translate the universal philosophy into
context-specific behavioural objectives while remaining fully aligned
with the overall Game Model.
Level 3 | Sub-Principles
Sub-Principles provide operational guidance for recurring tactical
situations.
They refine broader principles without replacing them.
Their purpose is to improve behavioural clarity rather than increase

Level 4 | Behaviour
Behaviour represents the practical expression of every principle.
It is here that philosophy becomes observable football.
Players do not execute principles directly.
They express them through intelligent behaviour adapted to the current

6.3 Interaction Between Playing Principles
Playing Principles should never be understood as isolated concepts.
Football is not organised through independent behaviours operating
separately from one another.
Every principle continuously influences, supports, and constrains the
application of other principles.
Within the DPF framework, Playing Principles form an interconnected
behavioural network rather than a sequential checklist.
Their value emerges through interaction.
Not isolation.
Interdependence Rather Than Independence
No Playing Principle can consistently achieve its objective without the
support of complementary principles.
For example, creating width without providing depth limits progression.
Increasing mobility without maintaining balance may reduce collective
stability.
Applying pressure without preserving compactness weakens defensive
organisation.
Football therefore requires simultaneous coordination between
multiple principles.
Each principle acquires meaning through its relationship with the
others.

-- 192 of 613 --

Context Determines Priority
Although every principle remains valid, their relative importance
continuously changes according to the evolving System State.
During controlled possession, spatial occupation may become the
dominant concern.
Immediately after losing possession, compactness and immediate
pressure may temporarily assume greater importance.
As the situation changes, behavioural priorities change accordingly.
The principles themselves remain constant.
Only their operational priority evolves.
Behavioural Synchronisation
Collective organisation depends not only upon applying the correct
principle, but upon applying compatible principles simultaneously.
When teammates interpret the game through the same behavioural
logic, individual actions naturally complement one another.
This synchronisation enables the team to adapt collectively without
requiring predetermined movements.
The Game Model therefore coordinates principles before it coordinates
players.

-- 193 of 613 --

From Principles to Football
Observable football behaviour emerges through the continuous
interaction of multiple principles operating simultaneously.
Successful attacks rarely result from a single principle.
Effective defending cannot be explained by compactness alone.
Likewise, successful transitions depend upon the coordinated
application of several behavioural priorities.
Football performance is therefore best understood as the emergent
product of interacting principles rather than isolated tactical actions.
The DPF Perspective
Within DPF, no Playing Principle should ever be analysed independently
of the behavioural network to which it belongs.
Every principle both influences and is influenced by others.
This interconnected structure enables the Game Model to remain
coherent while continuously adapting to changing environmental
conditions.
The effectiveness of the system therefore depends upon the quality of
the relationships between principles rather than the isolated execution
of any individual principle.

Playing Principles do more than organise individual behaviours.
Collectively, they shape the identity of the team.
A team's Playing Identity should not be understood as the
repetition of identical tactical actions.
Nor should it be reduced to possession statistics, pressing
intensity, or preferred formations.
Identity emerges when shared principles consistently influence
football behaviour across different opponents, match contexts,
and competitive environments.
Within the DPF framework, Playing Identity is therefore the
observable expression of the Game Model.
It is not created by isolated tactical ideas.
It is generated through the continuous application of coherent
behavioural principles.

-- 197 of 613 --

Identity Through Consistency
Every team encounters different situations.
Different opponents.
Different spaces.
Different constraints.
Different moments.
If the team's behaviour changes completely in response to every
circumstance, no recognisable identity exists.
Conversely, if behaviour remains guided by the same principles despite
contextual variation, identity becomes visible.
Consistency therefore refers to behavioural logic rather than tactical
repetition.
Identity Through Adaptation
Consistency should never be confused with rigidity.
Within DPF, Playing Identity remains stable precisely because players
continuously adapt.
Adaptation protects identity.
It does not threaten it.
Players modify their actions.
They do not abandon their principles.
Consequently, the external appearance of football may change while its

📘 Chapter VII
The Phases of Play
Understanding Football as a Continuous Cycle
7.1 Introduction
Football is often divided into separate phases for analytical purposes.
Teams attack.
Teams defend.
Possession is won.
Possession is lost.
Such classifications provide useful organisational references.
However, they should never suggest that football itself is played in
isolated segments.
Within the DPF framework, football is understood as a continuous
dynamic process in which every phase naturally evolves into the next.
There are no true beginnings.
There are no true endings.
Every action immediately creates the conditions for the next.
For this reason, the phases of play should not be interpreted as
independent tactical events.
They represent different expressions of the same continuously evolving
system.

-- 202 of 613 --

The Four Phases
Within Dynamic Positional Football, football is organised through four
fundamental phases:
In Possession
The team controls the ball and seeks to create, exploit, and progress
through functional advantages while preserving collective organisation.
Offensive Transition
The team has just regained possession.
The immediate objective is to stabilise the system, recognise emerging
opportunities, and determine the most appropriate attacking response.
Out of Possession
The opponent controls possession.
The team's objective becomes protecting functional space, limiting
opponent progression, and recovering possession while maintaining
collective organisation.
Defensive Transition
The team has just lost possession.
Immediate behavioural adaptation becomes essential in order to
prevent instability and preserve System Continuity.

8.1 Introduction
Possession should never be considered an objective in itself.
Within the DPF framework, possession represents a means through
which the team organises the game, manipulates the opponent, and
creates conditions that increase the probability of achieving functional
superiority.
Maintaining possession without purpose offers little competitive value.
Equally, direct progression without sufficient organisation often
increases instability.
The objective is therefore neither to circulate the ball indefinitely nor to
attack recklessly.
The objective is to use possession intelligently.
Within DPF, possession is understood as a dynamic process of
continuous organisation.
Every pass.
Every movement.
Every positional adjustment.
Every decision.
Contributes to shaping the evolving System State.

Players do not simply move the ball.

Consequently, successful possession depends not upon technical
execution alone, but upon collective behavioural coordination.
The team seeks to maximise functional advantages while preserving
System Continuity.
Possession therefore becomes an organisational tool rather than a
statistical outcome.
The Purpose of Possession
Within Dynamic Positional Football, possession serves multiple
interconnected purposes:
 To establish collective organisation.
 To manipulate the opponent.
 To create and exploit functional space.
 To control the tempo of the game.
 To improve decision quality.
 To prepare favourable transitions.
 To preserve System Continuity.

retained.

8.2 Functional Occupation of Space
Football is played in space.
However, space possesses no inherent tactical value.
Its significance depends entirely upon how it influences the
behaviour of both teams within the evolving System State.
Within the DPF framework, players are therefore not instructed
merely to occupy space.
They are required to occupy space functionally.
Functional Occupation of Space represents one of the
fundamental Playing Principles of Dynamic Positional Football.
Its objective is to organise the team in ways that maximise
collective effectiveness while continuously influencing the
behaviour of the opponent.
Space is not occupied because it is empty.
It is occupied because it performs a tactical function.
Every position adopted by a player should contribute to the
organisation of the collective system.
A position that fails to improve the functioning of the team
possesses little value regardless of its geometric correctness.
Consequently, positional occupation is evaluated according to
its functional contribution rather than its visual appearance.

-- 214 of 613 --

Definition
Functional Occupation of Space is the intentional positioning of
players to maximise the team's collective organisation by creating,
preserving, or exploiting functional advantages within the evolving
System State.
Purpose
The purpose of Functional Occupation of Space is not simply to
distribute players across the pitch.
Its objective is to influence the behaviour of teammates and opponents
simultaneously.
Effective occupation improves passing options.
Creates superiorities.
Facilitates progression.
Supports defensive stability.
Enhances collective adaptability.
Most importantly, it strengthens System Continuity.
Behavioural Objective
Players continuously evaluate whether their current position
contributes positively to the organisation of the system.
Whenever their position ceases to perform a functional role, adaptation
becomes necessary.
Movement therefore exists to improve functionality rather than to
satisfy predetermined positional patterns.

Functional Occupation of Space provides the structural foundation upon

Width becomes functional only when it stretches defensive

defensive line.
Support exists only when positioning improves decision-making.
Mobility acquires value only when movement increases collective

Every subsequent principle therefore operates through the quality of
spatial occupation.
Common Errors
Several common misconceptions reduce the effectiveness of positional
organisation.
Occupying space simply because it appears empty often disconnects
players from the collective structure.
Maintaining fixed positions regardless of the evolving context reduces
adaptability.
Conversely, excessive movement without functional purpose creates
instability rather than superiority.
Within DPF, movement is evaluated according to its contribution to the

Training environments should continuously challenge players to
recognise the functional value of their positioning.

 Does it strengthen available passing networks?
 Does it improve future options?
 Does it preserve System Continuity?
These questions gradually transform positional occupation into
intelligent football behaviour.

8.5 Functional Width
Width has traditionally been associated with stretching the
opponent horizontally.
While this objective remains important, the DPF framework
considers width to possess a broader functional purpose.
Players do not create width simply by positioning themselves
near the touchline.
They create width by influencing the behaviour of the opponent
in ways that improve the organisation of the collective system.
Functional Width therefore represents a behavioural principle
rather than a positional instruction.
Its value depends not upon location alone, but upon the tactical
function that width performs within the evolving System State.
Definition
Functional Width is the intentional horizontal expansion of the team's
structure to manipulate defensive organisation, create functional
space, and improve collective decision-making.

-- 228 of 613 --

Purpose
The primary purpose of Functional Width is to enlarge the opponent's
defensive problem.
Increasing horizontal spacing forces defenders to make more difficult
decisions regarding compactness, marking, and coverage.
As defensive lines expand, new functional spaces emerge between
players and units.
These spaces improve progression opportunities while simultaneously
preserving collective organisation.
Functional Width therefore supports both attacking development and
structural stability.
Behavioural Objective
Players continuously evaluate whether increasing or reducing width
improves the functioning of the collective system.
Maintaining maximum width at every moment is neither necessary nor
desirable.
The objective is to provide the appropriate width required by the
evolving situation.
Width should expand the opponent.
Not the distance between teammates unnecessarily.

Facilitates progression.
Maintains circulation.
Improves stability following possession loss.

security.

Supporting players continuously adjust their positioning according to

Football superiority is often misunderstood as a numerical
concept.
While having more players in a particular area may create an

effective football.

positioning.
A player occupying the correct functional position may
influence the game more effectively than several players
positioned incorrectly.
For this reason, Positional Superiority represents one of the
most fundamental mechanisms through which collective
organisation generates tactical advantage.
The objective is not to place players everywhere.
The objective is to place the right player in the right
functional location at the right moment.
Definition

intelligent positioning that provides greater tactical influence than the
opponent within the evolving System State.

-- 243 of 613 --

Purpose

capacity to solve tactical problems before physical actions become
necessary.

Improves receiving conditions.
Expands future options.
Forces defensive adjustments.
Generates time for decision-making.
In many situations, positional superiority allows the team to
dominate without requiring numerical superiority.
Behavioural Objective
Players continuously seek positions that maximise their influence
on the collective system.
The objective is not merely to receive the ball.
It is to occupy positions that increase the quality of future decisions
for the entire team.
Positioning therefore becomes proactive rather than reactive.
Players anticipate where functional advantage is likely to emerge
before it becomes visible.

8.10 Qualitative Superiority
Football is ultimately decided by players.
Regardless of tactical organisation, decisive moments often
depend upon the ability of individuals to outperform direct
opponents.
Within the DPF framework, however, individual quality is never
viewed in isolation.
The objective is not simply to rely upon talented players.
The objective is to create conditions in which individual
qualities can be expressed at the most influential moments.
Qualitative Superiority therefore represents the deliberate
alignment of individual strengths with favourable tactical
situations.
The system exists to maximise the value of the player.
The player, in turn, strengthens the system.
Definition
Qualitative Superiority is the intentional creation of situations in
which a player's individual qualities provide a decisive functional
advantage over the opponent within the evolving System State.

-- 253 of 613 --

Purpose
The purpose of Qualitative Superiority is to maximise the impact of
individual talent without compromising collective organisation.
Some players excel in one-versus-one situations.
Others possess exceptional vision, passing range, acceleration,
finishing ability, or decision-making.
Within DPF, these qualities are not expected to solve every problem
independently.
Instead, the collective system continuously seeks opportunities to
expose these strengths under favourable conditions.
The objective is not heroism.
It is optimisation.
Behavioural Objective
Players should recognise not only their own strengths but also the
strengths of their teammates.
Whenever the evolving System State creates favourable conditions,
the collective system should naturally direct the game toward the
player most capable of exploiting the situation.
The team therefore creates opportunities.
The individual completes them.

-- 254 of 613 --

structural principles.
Functional Occupation of Space establishes organisation.
Dynamic Mobility reshapes it.
Connectivity preserves it.
Width and Depth manipulate the opponent.
Positional Superiority creates influence.
Numerical Superiority creates additional options.
Only then does Qualitative Superiority fully emerge.
Within DPF, individual brilliance is not isolated from the collective
structure.
It is enabled by it.
Common Errors
One common misconception is expecting talented players to solve
tactical problems without organisational support.
Another involves forcing the ball toward star players regardless of the
evolving context.
Within DPF, individual quality should appear naturally through the
organisation of the system rather than through tactical dependency.
The team should create the opportunity.
Not chase it.

improvisation rather than collective intelligence.

Time improves perception.
Perception improves decisions.

create a local numerical superiority.

defensive structure.

isolated attacker receives under significantly improved conditions.
The objective is therefore not to change the side of play.
The objective is to relocate superiority.

intentionally created overload attracts the defensive block before
possession is transferred to isolate a teammate under superior
attacking conditions.

Purpose
The purpose of half-space progression is to create an attacking
environment where the ball carrier possesses the greatest variety of
progressive solutions while maintaining collective connectivity.
Rather than forcing direct penetration or predictable wide attacks,
progression through the half-space continuously increases tactical
flexibility and reduces defensive certainty.
Key Principles
Occupy Functional Space
The half-space should never be occupied because of its location alone.
Players should occupy it only when doing so improves the collective
structure and creates superior attacking conditions.

Receive with Open Body Orientation
Half-space progression becomes significantly more effective when the

wide channel.
Open body orientation transforms reception into immediate
progression by reducing decision time and increasing forward options.

Maintain Multiple Progressive Options
The primary value of the half-space lies in optionality.

 Central combination.
 Wide progression.
 Ball carrying.
 Backward circulation when necessary.
The objective is not simply to possess the ball.
The objective is to maximise the number of intelligent decisions
available.
Connect Central and Wide Progression
The half-space functions as the natural connector between central and
wide attacks.
From this corridor, the collective can alternate between interior
penetration and exterior exploitation without disrupting possession or
losing structural organisation.
Rather than forcing a choice between central or wide play, the half-
space preserves access to both simultaneously.

possibilities.
Freedom of movement produces freedom of decision.
Create Defensive Dilemmas
Progression through the half-space continuously places defenders in
situations of uncertainty.
The defender must decide whether to:
 Press aggressively.
 Protect the central corridor.
 Cover the wide channel.
 Maintain defensive compactness.
Every hesitation creates opportunities for the attacking collective.
The objective is not to beat the defender through speed alone.
It is to overload the defender's decision-making process.

quickly or slowly.
Tempo is understood as the collective ability to adapt the speed of play
in order to maximise tactical advantage while preserving System
Continuity.
Acceleration without superiority creates instability.
Patience without purpose destroys momentum.
The intelligent collective constantly adjusts its tempo to match the
tactical demands of the moment.

Tempo Control is the collective regulation of the speed of possession

Continuity.

attacking conditions.
The intelligent collective controls not only where and when the

Introduction
The most dangerous attacking movements are often the ones the
defender never sees.
Elite attackers rarely attempt to outrun defenders from positions of
direct confrontation.
Instead, they manipulate the defender's field of vision before attacking
the space that temporarily disappears from defensive awareness.
Within Dynamic Positional Football, the blind-side run is understood as
a behavioural manipulation rather than merely a running pattern.
The objective is not simply to arrive behind the defender.
The objective is to arrive without triggering an effective defensive
reaction.
Successful blind-side movement exploits perception before exploiting
space.
Definition
A Blind-Side Run is an attacking movement performed outside the
defender's immediate visual field in order to create temporary
separation and receive possession with positional advantage.

The purpose of the blind-side run is to reduce defensive reaction time
by attacking the defender's visual blind zone.

attacker gains advantage through superior timing, positioning, and
perception.

Attack the Defender's Blind Side
The run should begin from a position where the defender cannot
simultaneously observe both the attacker and the ball.
The greater the visual conflict imposed on the defender, the greater the
attacking advantage.
Synchronise with Ball Progression
Blind-side movement should never occur independently.

maximise control while minimising uncertainty.

accelerates collective reactions, and forces the opponent to operate
within increasingly restricted space.

An organised 10 can outperform a disorganised 11.
The objective is therefore to maximise functional superiority, not
merely numerical superiority.
Performance Indicators
Effective numerical situation management demonstrates:
 Rapid recognition of overloads.
 Efficient exploitation of superiority.
 Stable compactness during inferiority.
 Intelligent spacing.
 Collective adaptation.
 Minimal emotional disruption.

It is won by using them better.

Every mistake...

Teams that lose emotional control frequently lose tactical organisation

The objective is therefore not to suppress emotion.
The objective is to ensure that emotion never replaces decision-making.

The final minutes of a football match demand the highest levels

Matches are often decided not by how teams begin...

Within Dynamic Positional Football, closing the match is not

final whistle.
The objective is not merely to survive.
The objective is to finish the game with the same intelligence
that shaped it.

Chapter I
Introduction to the DPF Playbook
1.1 Purpose of the Playbook
The DPF Playbook is the practical implementation guide of the Dynamic
Positional Football (DPF) philosophy.
While the DPF Philosophy Manual defines the principles that shape the
identity of the model, and the DPF Game Model explains how the game
should be played, this Playbook focuses on one essential question:
How is the DPF Game Model translated into everyday coaching
practice?
It provides coaches, technical directors, academies, and football
organizations with a structured operational framework for designing,
delivering, and evaluating football training based on DPF principles.
1.2 What This Playbook Is
The Playbook is not a collection of drills.
It is an operational coaching guide that connects football philosophy,
tactical concepts, training methodology, and practical implementation
into one integrated system.
Every exercise, coaching intervention, session design, and learning
objective should reinforce the same football identity.

-- 9 of 303 --

1.3 Playbook vs. Tactical Manual
A Tactical Manual explains tactical concepts and describes how a team
should behave during different phases of play.
The DPF Playbook goes further.
It explains how those tactical concepts are taught, trained, evaluated,
and continuously improved within the DPF methodology.
A Tactical Manual answers:
What should the team do?
The DPF Playbook answers:
How do we build a team capable of doing it consistently?
For this reason, the term Playbook better represents the operational
nature of this publication.

-- 10 of 303 --

1.4 Relationship to the DPF Ecosystem
The Playbook should never be used as a standalone document.
It operates alongside the other core DPF publications:
• The Constitution establishes the governing philosophy.
• The Way explains the cultural and philosophical identity.
• Blueprint defines the organizational architecture.
• Institutional Framework defines governance and operational
structure.
• Game Model defines how football should be played.
• Playbook explains how that Game Model is implemented on the
training ground.
Together, these publications form one unified football operating system.
1.5 Guiding Principle
Ideas do not change football. Daily practice does.
The purpose of this Playbook is to ensure that every training
session becomes a direct expression of the DPF philosophy,
transforming principles into habits, habits into behaviors, and
behaviors into a recognizable football identity.

-- 11 of 303 --

Chapter II
How to Use This Playbook
2.1 Purpose of This Chapter
The DPF Playbook is designed as a practical working manual rather than
a book to be read from beginning to end.
Coaches, technical directors, analysts, educators, and football
organizations may enter the Playbook from different sections depending
on their roles and operational needs.
This chapter explains how to navigate and apply the Playbook
effectively.
2.2 Who Should Use This Playbook?
This Playbook is intended for:
• Football Coaches
• Technical Directors
• Academy Directors
• Performance Analysts
• Coach Educators
• Football Federations
• Professional Clubs
• Youth Academies
• Universities and Football Education Programs

-- 12 of 303 --

Although individual players may benefit from some concepts, the
Playbook is primarily written for professionals responsible for designing
and delivering football development.
2.3 How the Playbook Is Organized
The Playbook follows the same logical flow used within the DPF
methodology.
Each chapter builds upon the previous one, moving from principles to
practical application.
Typical chapter structure includes:
• Objective
• Key Principles
• Operational Guidelines
• Coaching Points
• Training Applications
• Common Mistakes
• Best Practices
• Evaluation Criteria
This consistent format allows readers to locate information quickly and
apply it immediately on the training ground.

-- 13 of 303 --

2.4 How to Read This Playbook
The Playbook can be used in three different ways:
As a learning resource
To understand the DPF coaching methodology.
As a planning guide
To prepare sessions, microcycles, and seasonal development plans.
As an operational reference
To support daily coaching decisions during training and competition.
2.5 Cross-Reference System
Throughout the Playbook, references will connect readers to other DPF
publications whenever additional context is required.
For example:
• Philosophy → The Way
• Organizational implementation → Institutional Framework
• Playing principles → Game Model
This prevents duplication while maintaining consistency across the DPF
ecosystem.

-- 14 of 303 --

2.6 A Practical Manual
This Playbook is designed to be used on the training pitch as much as in
the classroom.
Readers are encouraged to adapt exercises to their environment while
preserving the core DPF principles.
The objective is not to copy sessions exactly, but to understand the logic
behind every exercise and reproduce the intended learning outcomes.

practice, support consistent decision-making, and ensure that every

Chapter III
The DPF Coaching Methodology
3.1 Introduction
The DPF Coaching Methodology defines how football should be taught,
learned, and continuously improved.
It is not simply a collection of coaching techniques. It is a complete
learning framework that transforms the DPF philosophy into daily
coaching practice.
Every training activity should develop the player's understanding of the
game while reinforcing the collective identity of the team.
3.2 Coaching as Learning Design
Within DPF, coaching is not the delivery of information.
It is the design of learning environments.
The coach does not create players by giving answers.
The coach creates situations where players discover better decisions
through interaction with the game.
Training therefore becomes a process of guided problem-solving rather
than repetitive instruction.

-- 16 of 303 --

3.3 Principles Before Exercises
Exercises are not the foundation of coaching.
Principles are.
The same exercise can produce completely different learning outcomes
depending on the coaching objective.
For this reason, every session begins with a principle, not with a drill.
The exercise exists only to serve the principle.
3.4 Representative Learning
Every training activity should represent the reality of football.
Players learn best when the information, space, time, pressure,
teammates, opponents, and decisions resemble those experienced
during competition.
The closer training resembles the game, the greater the transfer of
learning.

-- 17 of 303 --

3.5 Constraints-Based Coaching
Rather than constantly stopping play to give instructions, DPF encourages
coaches to manipulate the environment.
Examples include:
• Adjusting the size of the playing area.
• Limiting the number of touches.
• Creating numerical superiority or inferiority.
• Changing scoring conditions.
• Modifying time available for decision-making.
• Restricting or encouraging specific tactical behaviors.
Players learn by adapting to constraints rather than memorizing solutions.
3.6 Guided Discovery
Instead of providing immediate answers, coaches should encourage players
to think.
Questions such as:
• What did you see?
• Why was this option better?
• What could you change next time?
help players develop independent tactical understanding.
The objective is not obedience.
The objective is intelligent decision-making.

-- 18 of 303 --

3.7 Feedback Philosophy
Feedback should improve future performance rather than simply
evaluate past actions.
Effective feedback is:
• Timely
• Specific
• Objective
• Actionable
• Connected to DPF principles
Feedback should guide learning without interrupting the natural rhythm
of training unnecessarily.
3.8 Building Autonomous Players
The ultimate objective of coaching is not dependence on the coach.
It is player autonomy.
A successful DPF player can:
• Read the game.
• Solve problems independently.
• Adapt to changing situations.
• Support teammates.
• Maintain the team's collective identity under pressure.

-- 19 of 303 --

Chapter Summary
The DPF Coaching Methodology is built on one central belief:
Great coaching does not produce players who follow
instructions. It produces players who understand the game
well enough to make the right decisions without waiting for
instructions.

-- 20 of 303 --

Chapter IV
Session Design Framework
4.1 Introduction
Every training session should be intentionally designed.
Within DPF, sessions are not built by selecting random exercises. They
are structured learning experiences created to develop specific game
principles through representative football situations.
Each session must contribute to the long-term development of both the
individual player and the collective team.
4.2 The Objective Comes First
Every session begins with one clear learning objective.
Examples include:
• Building from the back under pressure.
• Pressing after losing possession.
• Creating overloads in wide areas.
• Improving positional occupation.
• Developing third-man combinations.
Everything else in the session should support this objective.

-- 21 of 303 --

4.3 The DPF Session Structure
A typical DPF session follows a logical progression:
1. Session Briefing
2. Dynamic Activation
3. Technical Preparation
4. Tactical Learning Activity
5. Representative Small-Sided Games
6. Expanded Game Scenarios
7. Match Application
8. Reflection and Debrief
Each phase prepares players for the next, gradually increasing complexity and
decision-making demands.
4.4 Progression of Complexity
Training should evolve from simpler situations to more complex ones.
Progression may involve:
• Increasing the number of players.
• Enlarging the playing area.
• Adding opponents.
• Introducing transition moments.
• Increasing decision-making speed.
• Removing constraints as players improve.
Learning should never jump ahead of the players' understanding.

-- 22 of 303 --

4.5 Designing Representative Tasks
Every exercise should answer three questions:
• Which game principle does it develop?
• Which decisions are players required to make?
• How closely does it represent real match situations?
If an activity cannot answer these questions, it should be redesigned.
4.6 Coaching During the Session
The coach should intervene only when it improves learning.
Possible interventions include:
• Guided questioning.
• Individual feedback.
• Team corrections.
• Freeze moments.
• Live coaching.
• Silent observation.
The timing of the intervention is often as important as the intervention
itself.

-- 23 of 303 --

4.7 Evaluating the Session
A successful session is not measured by intensity alone.
Evaluation should consider:
• Achievement of learning objectives.
• Quality of decision-making.
• Tactical understanding.
• Transfer to realistic game situations.
• Player engagement.
• Consistency with DPF principles.
Chapter Summary
Every DPF training session is designed with purpose.
Rather than asking, "What drills should we do today?", the DPF coach
asks:
"What should our players learn today, and what is the best football
environment for them to learn it?"

Chapter V
Training Components
5.1 Introduction
Every DPF training session is built from a combination of interconnected
learning components.
Each component serves a specific developmental purpose while contributing
to the overall objectives of the session.
No component exists in isolation.
Together, they create a complete learning experience that reflects the
demands of the game.
5.2 Dynamic Activation
The session begins by preparing players physically, mentally, and cognitively.
Dynamic activation should include:
• Movement preparation
• Mobility
• Coordination
• Ball interaction
• Perception and scanning
• Decision-making from the very beginning
Players should enter the football context immediately rather than separating
physical preparation from the game.

-- 25 of 303 --

5.3 Technical Development
Technical actions are developed within realistic football situations.
Examples include:
• Passing
• Receiving
• Dribbling
• Finishing
• Heading
• Ball Protection
Technique should never be trained independently from perception,
decision-making, and tactical context whenever possible.
5.4 Tactical Learning
This is the core of every DPF session.
Training activities should develop:
• Individual Principles
• Unit Principles
• Team Principles
• Phase Principles
• Collective Behaviors
Every activity must connect directly to the DPF Game Model.

-- 26 of 303 --

5.5 Small-Sided Games (SSGs)
Small-Sided Games are the primary learning environment within DPF.
They provide:
• More ball contacts
• More decisions
• Higher tactical repetition
• Greater player involvement
• Better learning transfer
Game constraints should be adjusted according to the objective rather
than fixed by tradition.
5.6 Position-Specific Development
While maintaining collective identity, players should also develop the
unique demands of their positions.
Training should address:
• Positional responsibilities
• Functional relationships
• Position-specific decision-making
• Role adaptability
Players learn both their role and their contribution to the collective
system.

-- 27 of 303 --

5.7 Match Application
The final stage of the session should recreate the complexity of competition.
Players are encouraged to apply everything learned under realistic match
conditions with minimal coach intervention.
This phase allows coaches to evaluate learning transfer rather than isolated
execution.
5.8 Reflection and Review
Learning continues after the final whistle.
Players and coaches should review:
• What was learned?
• What improved?
• What remains challenging?
• Which principles require further development?
Reflection transforms experience into long-term learning.

Part II
Training the Game Model
Chapter VI
Training In Possession
6.1 Introduction
The attacking phase begins the moment possession is secured.
Within DPF, attacking is not simply the act of moving the ball forward. It is
the process of creating and exploiting advantages through intelligent
positioning, coordinated movement, and purposeful decision-making.
Every training activity in possession should reinforce the principles defined in
the DPF Game Model.
6.2 Objectives of Possession
The primary objectives of possession are to:
• Control the game.
• Progress the ball.
• Create and exploit superiority.
• Manipulate the opponent.
• Access dangerous spaces.
• Create goal-scoring opportunities.
• Score goals while maintaining collective stability.
Possession is never an objective by itself.
It is a tool to achieve competitive superiority.

-- 29 of 303 --

6.3 Core Principles
Every possession exercise should reinforce one or more of the
following principles:
• Width
• Depth
• Support
• Mobility
• Positional Occupation
• Scanning
• Third-Man Combinations
• Creating Superiorities
• Overload to Isolate
• Tempo Control
• Penetration
• Rest Defence
These principles form the tactical language of DPF.

-- 30 of 303 --

6.4 Coaching Objectives
The coach should develop players capable of:
• Recognizing available space.
• Identifying numerical advantages.
• Understanding positional relationships.
• Choosing the best progression option.
• Maintaining team structure during possession.
• Adapting decisions under pressure.
Training should improve perception before execution.
6.5 Coaching Interventions
During possession practices, coaches should emphasize:
• Body orientation.
• Scanning before receiving.
• Timing of movement.
• Passing speed.
• Distance between players.
• Communication.
• Decision quality.
• Synchronization of movements.
Interventions should improve perception and decision-making rather than
merely correcting technical mistakes.

-- 31 of 303 --

6.6 Common Training Errors
Avoid sessions where:
• Players pass without purpose.
• Possession becomes repetitive.
• Space remains static.
• Players move after the pass instead of before.
• Numerical superiority is ignored.
• Exercises lack opposition.
• Decisions are predetermined.
Training should always preserve the uncertainty of the game.
6.7 Transition to Practical Application
The following chapters break the attacking phase into its operational components.
Each chapter presents:
• Tactical objectives.
• Coaching points.
• Representative practices.
• Session design examples.
• Common mistakes.
• Progressions.
• Evaluation criteria.
This allows coaches to systematically develop every stage of attacking play.

Every pass, movement, and decision should improve the team's position
while increasing the probability of creating an advantage.
The objective is not to keep the ball.
The objective is to use the ball intelligently.

Chapter VII
Training the Build Up
7.1 Introduction
The Build Up phase is the foundation of organized attacking play.
Its purpose is not simply to move the ball out of the defensive third, but
to establish control, manipulate the opposition, and create the
conditions for successful progression.
Within DPF, every Build Up exercise should develop intelligent players
capable of recognizing and exploiting advantages under pressure.
7.2 Learning Objectives
By the end of this phase, players should be able to:
• Build confidently under pressure.
• Maintain possession with purpose.
• Create numerical superiority.
• Recognize pressing triggers.
• Exploit free players.
• Progress through or around pressure.
• Preserve the team's attacking structure.

-- 34 of 303 --

7.3 Tactical Principles
Training activities should reinforce the following principles:
• Width in the first line.
• Depth through supporting players.
• Proper spacing.
• Body orientation.
• Scanning before receiving.
• Third-man combinations.
• Creating passing lanes.
• Attracting pressure to release space.
• Switching the point of attack.
• Patience with purpose.

-- 35 of 303 --

7.4 Representative Training Practices
The Build Up phase should be developed through representative
football situations rather than isolated passing drills.
Examples include:
• Positional Rondos
• Build Up vs High Press
• Numerical Superiority Games
• Directional Possession Games
• Goalkeeper Integration Exercises
• Functional Unit Practices
• Phase-of-Play Scenarios
Each activity should reproduce the information and decisions players
experience during competition.

-- 36 of 303 --

7.5 Coaching Interventions
The coach should observe and intervene around key moments such as:
• First touch direction.
• Receiving on the back foot.
• Scanning before the pass.
• Distance between teammates.
• Speed of circulation.
• Timing of support.
• Recognition of overloads.
• Decision quality under pressure.
Questions often produce better learning than immediate corrections.
7.6 Common Errors
Typical Build Up problems include:
• Standing in straight lines.
• Supporting too close to the ball.
• Slow circulation.
• Playing without scanning.
• Forcing vertical passes.
• Ignoring the free player.
• Breaking team structure.
Training should expose these problems naturally and help players solve them.

• Increasing numerical equality.
• Expanding toward full-team scenarios.
Progression should challenge decision-making without sacrificing learning quality.

Coaches should evaluate:
• Quality of positional occupation.
• Speed of decision-making.
• Success against pressure.
• Ability to create superiority.
• Communication.
• Ball circulation efficiency.
• Successful progression into the midfield.
• Collective organization.
• Performance should be judged by the quality of decisions, not only by
successful passes.

Chapter VIII
Training Progression
8.1 Introduction
Progression is the process of advancing the ball and the team from the
build-up phase into advanced attacking areas while maintaining control,
structure, and collective balance.
Within DPF, progression is not measured by the number of forward
passes. It is measured by the team's ability to move into more
advantageous positions while preserving the conditions for continued
attack and defensive stability.
8.2 Learning Objectives
By the end of this phase, players should be able to:
• Progress through, around, or over defensive pressure.
• Identify the most effective progression route.
• Exploit positional and numerical superiority.
• Maintain spacing and team connectivity.
• Recognize the correct moment to accelerate play.
• Protect possession while advancing toward the attacking third.

-- 53 of 303 --

8.3 Tactical Principles
Training should reinforce:
• Vertical progression.
• Third-man combinations.
• Overload to Isolate.
• Switching Play.
• Width and Depth.
• Positional Rotation.
• Timing of movement.
• Passing lane creation.
• Supporting angles.
• Rest Defence.
These principles help players advance the game with purpose
rather than speed alone.

• Speed of circulation.

8.6 Common Errors
Typical progression problems include:
• Forcing vertical passes.
• Ignoring overloads.
• Poor spacing between lines.
• Slow support.
• Predictable circulation.
• Lack of width.
• Progressing without securing defensive balance.
These mistakes should become learning opportunities rather than
reasons to stop training repeatedly.
8.7 Practice Progressions
Exercises may increase in difficulty by:
• Reducing space.
• Increasing defensive pressure.
• Removing touch limitations.
• Adding transition rules.
• Introducing directional constraints.
• Expanding from unit practices to full-team scenarios.
Complexity should increase while preserving decision quality.

8.8 Evaluation Criteria
Progression should be evaluated through:
• Successful line-breaking actions.
• Effective use of overloads.
• Progression into advanced zones.
• Decision quality.
• Ball circulation efficiency.
• Positional discipline.
• Team connectivity.
• Maintenance of Rest Defence.
Chapter Summary
Progression is the bridge between controlled possession and attacking
opportunity.
A successful DPF team advances the game intelligently, selecting the
most effective route based on the evolving conditions of the match
rather than following predetermined patterns.

exploit, and finish attacking situations with maximum efficiency.

highest levels of pressure.

By the end of this phase, players should be able to:

• Finish attacks efficiently.

Chapter X
Training Finishing
10.1 Introduction
Finishing is the final action of the attacking phase.
Within DPF, finishing is not viewed as an isolated technical skill. It is the
product of intelligent movement, effective positioning, precise timing,
and correct decision-making under pressure.
The objective is not simply to shoot, but to maximize the probability of
scoring.
10.2 Learning Objectives
By the end of this phase, players should be able to:
• Recognize high-quality shooting opportunities.
• Select the appropriate finishing technique.
• Finish under defensive pressure.
• Finish with minimal touches.

11.1 Introduction
Defending begins the moment possession is lost.
Within DPF, defending is a collective process of protecting space, controlling
the opponent, and creating the conditions to regain possession. The
objective is not merely to stop attacks, but to reduce the opponent's options
while preserving the team's compactness and readiness to transition.
Every defensive action should reinforce the collective identity of the team.

By the end of this phase, players should be able to:
• Defend collectively.
• Maintain compactness.
• Protect central spaces.
• Recognize pressing opportunities.
• Delay attacks when necessary.
• Communicate effectively.
• Regain possession in an organized manner.

• Collective shifting.
• Defensive patience.
• Rest Defence.

opportunities to regain possession.

• Reduce the opponent's available space.
• Force predictable decisions.
• Regain possession efficiently.
• Protect the team's defensive balance.
• Transition immediately after ball recovery.

14.1 Introduction
The Low Block is a defensive organization designed to protect the area
closest to goal, minimize dangerous spaces, and force the opponent into
low-probability attacking actions.
Within DPF, the Low Block is not passive defending. It is an organized
collective strategy that prioritizes compactness, discipline, communication,
and readiness to transition immediately after regaining possession.
The objective is to defend intelligently while remaining capable of launching
effective counter-attacks.

A turnover begins the instant possession changes.

imbalance created by the loss of possession.
The first seconds after the turnover often determine the outcome of the
next phase.

By the end of this phase, players should be able to:
• React immediately after losing possession.
• Recognize when to counter-press.
• Delay the opponent if recovery is impossible.
• Protect central spaces.
• Recover defensive organization quickly.
• Communicate effectively during transition.
• Make rapid decisions under pressure.

Attacking Transition begins the instant possession is regained.

opponent's temporary disorganization before they recover their
defensive structure. Players must recognize whether to attack
immediately, maintain possession, or stabilize the game according to
the context.

intelligence.

By the end of this phase, players should be able to:
• Recognize opportunities immediately after regaining possession.
• Attack quickly when numerical or positional superiority exists.
• Maintain possession when immediate progression is not possible.

• Support the ball carrier effectively.
• Create goal-scoring opportunities from transitions.
• Organize attacking structure during the transition.

• Transition Awareness.

Football is learned through football.
Within DPF, match-based training represents the highest level of

Chapter XXI
The DPF Coach
21.1 Introduction
A football methodology is only as effective as the coach who applies it.
Within DPF, the coach is more than an instructor. The coach is a
designer of learning environments, a guide for player development, and
the guardian of the team's football identity.
The coach's responsibility is not to control every action, but to create
conditions that allow intelligent football to emerge.
21.2 The Role of the DPF Coach
The DPF Coach should:
• Develop players before developing results.
• Protect the DPF playing identity.
• Design representative learning environments.
• Encourage intelligent decision-making.
• Foster continuous improvement.
• Lead through clarity, consistency, and professionalism.

-- 285 of 303 --

21.3 Core Coaching Principles
Every DPF Coach should embrace:
• Player-Centered Development.
• Representative Learning.
• Tactical Understanding Before Technical Perfection.
• Guided Discovery.
• Continuous Feedback.
• Long-Term Development.
• Collective Responsibility.
• Adaptability.
• Lifelong Learning.
21.4 Leadership Responsibilities
The coach is responsible for:
• Building a positive learning culture.
• Establishing clear behavioral standards.
• Promoting teamwork and accountability.
• Supporting individual growth.
• Communicating effectively with players and staff.
• Inspiring commitment to the Game Model.

-- 286 of 303 --

21.5 Professional Behaviors
A DPF Coach should consistently demonstrate:
• Preparation.
• Integrity.
• Respect.
• Discipline.
• Curiosity.
• Emotional Control.
• Effective Communication.
• Reflective Practice.
21.6 Self-Evaluation
After every session and every match, the coach should reflect:
• Did today's training solve a football problem?
• Did players make better decisions?
• Was the learning environment representative?
• Did I coach too much or too little?
• What will I improve next time?
Reflection is essential for continuous coaching development.

-- 287 of 303 --

Chapter Summary
The DPF Coach is not defined by formations, trophies, or training
exercises.
The DPF Coach is defined by the ability to develop intelligent players,
cohesive teams, and a sustainable football identity through purposeful
coaching and continuous learning.

-- 289 of 303 --

Final Reflection
Football has never been a finished game.
Every generation discovers new ideas, challenges existing
beliefs, and leaves its own contribution to the evolution of the
sport.
The purpose of the DPF Playbook is not to provide fixed
answers for every situation. Instead, it offers a practical
framework that helps coaches design representative learning
environments, develop intelligent players, and build teams with
a clear and sustainable identity.
No methodology should ever become a limitation to innovation.
Every training session, every match, and every season presents
an opportunity to observe, learn, adapt, and improve.
The future of football will belong to those who remain curious
enough to question, disciplined enough to learn, and
courageous enough to evolve.
The game never ends. Football has never stopped evolving.

-- 290 of 303 --
