Chapter 9
Physical Curriculum
9.1 Introduction
Physical performance is a fundamental component of long-term
player development.
Within the DPF Academy, physical development is not treated as
isolated fitness training. Instead, it is integrated into football
learning, ensuring that every physical quality supports technical
execution, tactical understanding, and match performance.
Players are prepared for the demands of the game through
representative football environments.
9.2 Purpose of the Physical Curriculum
The Physical Curriculum aims to:
• Develop age-appropriate physical qualities.
• Improve movement efficiency.
• Build resilience against injury.
• Support technical and tactical performance.
• Prepare players for increasing match demands.
• Promote lifelong athletic development.
Physical preparation serves football, not the other way around.

Chapter 10
Social, Character & Professional Development
10.1 Introduction
A football player develops within a human and professional
environment.
Technical, tactical, physical, and psychological capabilities are
important, but they do not fully define the player who must
operate inside a team, academy, club, family, community, and
eventually the professional football industry.
DPF therefore considers social, character, and professional
development an essential component of the complete player.
The objective is to develop players who are not only capable
on the pitch, but increasingly capable of managing
themselves, their relationships, their responsibilities, and
their careers.
Develop the footballer. Develop the person. Prepare the
professional.

-- 81 of 866 --

10.2 The Social Dimension
Football is fundamentally relational.
Players constantly interact with:
• Teammates.
• Coaches.
• Opponents.
• Staff.
• Family.
• Friends.
• Club leadership.
• Support networks.
Social development therefore concerns the player's ability to
function effectively within these relationships.

-- 82 of 866 --

10.3 Communication
Players must progressively develop the ability to:
• Communicate clearly.
• Listen actively.
• Give information.
• Receive information.
• Ask questions.
• Express concerns.
• Communicate under pressure.
• Adapt communication to different people.
Communication is not simply a personality characteristic.
It is a football capability.

-- 83 of 866 --

10.4 Team Behavior
The individual player operates within collective objectives.
Development therefore includes:
• Cooperation.
• Trust.
• Responsibility.
• Respect.
• Supporting teammates.
• Accepting different roles.
• Contributing to team standards.
A talented player who consistently damages the collective
environment creates a developmental problem for both
themselves and the team.

-- 84 of 866 --

10.5 Character Development
Character is reflected through repeated behavior, especially
when circumstances become difficult.
DPF considers important character dimensions such as:
• Responsibility.
• Integrity.
• Discipline.
• Courage.
• Humility.
• Accountability.
• Respect.
• Persistence.
Character should not be taught primarily through slogans.
It should be developed through expectations, experiences,
decisions, consequences, and reflection.

-- 85 of 866 --

10.6 Accountability
Players progressively need to take responsibility for:
• Preparation.
• Training behavior.
• Recovery.
• Equipment.
• Time management.
• Communication.
• Learning.
• Performance.
• Professional conduct.
The developmental progression is:
External Accountability
→ Shared Accountability
→ Self-Accountability
The ultimate goal is a player who does not require constant
supervision to meet standards.

• Helping teammates.
• Maintaining standards.
• Taking responsibility during difficult moments.

-- 87 of 866 --

Professionalism begins before the player becomes a

• Punctuality.
• Preparation.
• Nutrition.
• Recovery.
• Sleep.
• Training standards.
• Personal organization.
• Communication.
• Respect.
• Learning.
Professional status should not be the moment when
professional behavior suddenly begins.

-- 88 of 866 --

10.9 Education & Personal Development
Player development must coexist with education and broader
personal growth.
Young players should develop:
• Academic responsibility.
• Communication skills.
• General knowledge.
• Financial awareness.
• Digital awareness.
• Social responsibility.
• Personal interests outside football.
The objective is not to distract the player from football.
It is to help create a more capable and resilient human being.

-- 89 of 866 --

10.10 Family & Support Network
Family can have a major influence on the player’s
development.
Positive support can provide:
• Stability.
• Encouragement.
• Perspective.
• Emotional support.
• Practical assistance.
However, excessive pressure can negatively affect:
• Confidence.
• Decision-making.
• Motivation.
• Player autonomy.
The DPF approach therefore seeks:
Support without control.

-- 90 of 866 --

10.11 The Player's Inner Circle
As the player develops, their support network may include:
• Family.
• Coaches.
• Academy staff.
• Performance specialists.
• Education staff.
• Medical professionals.
• Psychological professionals.
• Player representatives.
The player's interests should remain the central reference
point.
Different people may provide different forms of support.
No single person should automatically control the player's
entire development environment.

-- 91 of 866 --

relationship:
Player Representation.
An agent or player representative may support the player in
navigating the professional football environment.
This can include:
• Career guidance.
• Contract negotiation.
• Transfer opportunities.
• Professional representation.
• Communication with clubs.
• Career planning.
• Industry guidance.
• Protection of the player's interests.
However, representation should complement player
development, not replace it.

A responsible representative can help the player understand:

• Unrealistic promises.
• Financial pressure.
• Premature transfers.
• Excessive expectations.
• Poor professional advice.
• Conflicts of interest.
• Exploitative relationships.
Player representation should therefore include a protective

• Contracts.
• Decisions.
• Risks.
• Responsibilities.
• Professional consequences.
The objective is informed decision-making, not dependence.

The agent should not become the player's coach.

The development ecosystem should remain clear:

Develops football capability.
Academy
Creates the developmental environment.
Performance Team
Supports physical and performance development.
Family

Agent / Representative
Supports professional representation and career
management.
Player
Remains the central decision-maker and owner of their
pathway.
This separation protects the integrity of the development
system.

10.16 Player Ownership and Representation
As players mature, representation should strengthen player
autonomy rather than reduce it.
The progression should be:
Family-Led
→ Shared Understanding
→ Player-Informed
→ Player-Led
The representative should provide expertise while the player
increasingly understands and participates in major decisions.
Representation should increase the player's agency, not
replace it.

-- 96 of 866 --

10.17 Choosing a Representative
Players and families should evaluate potential representatives
through criteria such as:
• Integrity.
• Transparency.
• Experience.
• Communication.
• Professional network.
• Understanding of the player's development.
• Long-term orientation.
• Conflict-of-interest management.
• Respect for the player's autonomy.
• Alignment with the player's values.
Reputation alone should not determine the decision.
The quality of the relationship matters.

-- 97 of 866 --

10.18 Conflicts of Interest
Player representation can involve complex relationships.
Potential conflicts may emerge when:
• Multiple parties have competing interests.
• Commercial incentives influence advice.
• A short-term transfer benefits one party more than the
player.
• External relationships influence recommendations.
Players should therefore be encouraged to understand:
Who benefits from this decision?
and:
Is this decision aligned with my long-term development and
career?
Where appropriate, players should receive independent
professional advice.

• Contracts.
• Income.
• Expenses.

• Financial planning.
• Commercial opportunities.
• Personal brand.

• Privacy.

• Relationships.
• Opportunities.
• Sponsorship.
• Reputation.
• Career perception.

• Selection disappointment.
• Losses.
• Injury.
• Contract uncertainty.
• Criticism.
• Reduced playing time.
• Transfer decisions.

Can the player maintain standards when circumstances are

Chapter 11
Learning Capacity & Adaptability
11.1 Introduction
The ability to learn is one of the most important
characteristics in long-term player development.
Football continuously changes.
Opponents change.
Roles change.
Coaches change.
Physical demands change.
Competition levels change.
Therefore, a player who can only reproduce familiar solutions
may eventually reach the limits of their current capability.
DPF seeks to develop players who can learn, adapt, transfer,
and continue improving as demands evolve.
The ultimate development objective is not to create a player
who knows everything, but a player who knows how to
keep learning.

-- 110 of 866 --

11.2 What Is Learning Capacity?
Learning capacity is the player's ability to:
• Acquire new information.
• Understand new concepts.
• Experiment with solutions.
• Respond to feedback.
• Reflect on experience.
• Adapt behavior.
• Transfer learning into new contexts.
• Continue improving with increasing independence.
Learning capacity is therefore more than intelligence or
knowledge.
It is the player's ability to convert experience into improved
capability.

-- 111 of 866 --

Learning capacity is therefore more than intelligence or

-- 111 of 866 --

11.3 What Is Adaptability?
Adaptability is the ability to modify behavior effectively when
circumstances change.
A player may need to adapt to:
• A new opponent.
• A different tactical structure.
• A new position.
• A different role.
• Increased physical demands.
• Reduced time and space.
• A new coach.
• A higher competition level.
• Unexpected game situations.
Adaptability allows the player to remain functional when
familiar solutions are no longer sufficient.

-- 112 of 866 --

11.4 Learning and Adaptability Are Connected
Learning creates new possibilities.
Adaptability allows the player to use those possibilities in
changing environments.
The relationship can be represented as:
Experience
→ Learning
→ Adaptation
→ New Capability
→ New Experience
The cycle then repeats.

-- 113 of 866 --

11.5 The DPF Learning Cycle
The DPF learning process follows:
Experience
The player encounters a football problem.
↓
Perception
The player receives information from the environment.
↓
Action
The player attempts a solution.
↓
Outcome
The action produces a result.
↓
Reflection
The player evaluates what happened.
↓
Feedback
Additional information helps refine understanding.
↓
Adjustment
The player modifies behavior.
↓
Re-Experience
The player encounters the problem again under new conditions.
This is how experience becomes development.

-- 114 of 866 --

11.6 Learning Through Football Problems
Players learn most meaningfully when they encounter
problems that require them to perceive, decide, and act.
Instead of always providing the solution, the development
environment can create conditions in which the player must
discover:
What is happening?
What options exist?
Which solution is appropriate?
What changes if the situation changes?
This develops understanding rather than simple compliance.

-- 115 of 866 --

11.7 Exploration
Learning requires exploration.
Players need opportunities to:
• Try different solutions.
• Make decisions.
• Experience consequences.
• Compare alternatives.
• Discover effective behaviors.
Exploration does not mean unlimited freedom.
The coach establishes the environment, objectives,
constraints, and standards within which meaningful
exploration occurs.

-- 116 of 866 --

11.8 Variability
Repeating exactly the same solution under exactly the same
conditions can produce fragile learning.
DPF therefore values functional variability.
The same underlying problem may be presented through:
• Different spaces.
• Different opponents.
• Different starting positions.
• Different time constraints.
• Different numerical situations.
• Different game states.
This helps players develop solutions that can survive changing
conditions.

11.9 Transfer
Learning is incomplete if it remains trapped inside the
training environment.
Transfer occurs when the player can apply learning:
In Training
↓
In Representative Problems
↓
Under Pressure
↓
In Competition
↓
In New Contexts
The ultimate evidence of learning is therefore not simply:
"The player performed the drill correctly."
It is:
"The player can use the capability when the football
problem changes."

-- 118 of 866 --

11.10 Feedback
Feedback provides information that helps players understand
their performance and adjust future behavior.
Effective feedback can address:
• What happened.
• Why it happened.
• What was effective.
• What could change.
• What alternatives exist.
But feedback should not create dependency.
The developmental progression is:
Coach Gives Answer
→ Coach Guides Reflection
→ Player Evaluates
→ Player Self-Corrects
This connects directly to the DPF principle of Player
Ownership.

-- 119 of 866 --

11.11 Reflection
Reflection converts experience into understanding.
Players can be encouraged to ask:
• What happened?
• What did I perceive?
• What did I decide?
• Why?
• What worked?
• What did not?
• What would I change?
• What will I try next time?
Reflection should remain connected to football behavior
rather than becoming an abstract exercise.

-- 120 of 866 --

11.12 Metacognition
As players mature, they should increasingly understand how
they learn.
This includes awareness of:
• How they respond to feedback.
• What helps them understand.
• Where they struggle.
• How they prepare.
• How they solve problems.
• How they respond to mistakes.
This creates a higher level of player independence.
The player is no longer simply learning football.
The player is learning how they themselves learn football.

-- 121 of 866 --

11.13 Adaptability Under Pressure
Adaptability must eventually survive pressure.
Players may understand a solution during training but
struggle to reproduce it when:
• Time is reduced.
• Space is reduced.
• Opponents become stronger.
• Fatigue increases.
• Stakes increase.
• The game becomes unpredictable.
Therefore, adaptability should progressively be tested under
increasing levels of complexity.

-- 122 of 866 --

11.14 Cognitive Flexibility
Cognitive flexibility is the ability to reconsider an existing
solution when new information appears.
A player may initially expect:
Solution A
but recognize that the environment now requires:
Solution B
This is fundamental to football intelligence.
The player must be capable of abandoning an initially
reasonable plan when the situation changes.

-- 123 of 866 --

11.15 Learning From Failure
Failure can provide valuable information.
A failed action may reveal:
• Incorrect perception.
• Poor decision.
• Technical limitation.
• Timing problem.
• Misunderstanding.
• Inappropriate risk.
• Environmental difficulty.
The developmental response should therefore be:
Failure → Investigation → Learning → Adjustment
rather than:
Failure → Punishment → Avoidance
The objective is to preserve accountability while maintaining
learning.

11.16 Learning From Success
Success also requires reflection.
A player should understand:
• Why did it work?
• Which information mattered?
• Which decision created the advantage?
• Can the solution work again?
• Under what conditions would it fail?
This prevents successful actions from becoming accidental
habits.

-- 125 of 866 --

11.17 Curiosity
Curiosity supports long-term development.
Players who ask questions, explore possibilities, and seek
understanding are more likely to continue learning.
DPF therefore encourages:
• Questions.
• Exploration.
• Investigation.
• Experimentation.
• Reflection.
Curiosity should be supported by a structured environment
that maintains clear standards.

-- 126 of 866 --

11.18 Adaptability Across Positions and Roles
Exposure to different roles can expand a player's
understanding of the game.
When appropriate, players may benefit from experiencing:
• Different positions.
• Different responsibilities.
• Different tactical structures.
• Different game problems.
The objective is not necessarily to make every player multi-
positional.
It is to expand their football understanding and adaptability
where developmentally appropriate.

-- 127 of 866 --

11.19 Adaptability Across Competition Levels
Progression into stronger competition creates new learning
demands.
The player may encounter:
• Faster decisions.
• Stronger opponents.
• Less space.
• Greater tactical complexity.
• Higher physical intensity.
• Greater psychological pressure.
A player who adapts successfully demonstrates more than
current ability.
They demonstrate capacity to grow into a new environment.

-- 128 of 866 --

11.20 Learning Capacity and Potential
Learning capacity is an important component of
developmental potential.
A player's current capability tells us:
What can they do now?
Learning capacity helps us understand:
How might they respond to future development?
This does not mean learning capacity can predict a player's
future with certainty.
It means it provides important evidence about the player's
developmental trajectory.

-- 129 of 866 --

11.21 Learning Environment
Learning capacity is influenced by the environment.
A productive learning environment provides:
• Appropriate challenge.
• Meaningful problems.
• Feedback.
• Reflection.
• Repetition with variation.
• Psychological safety.
• Competition.
• Player ownership.
The environment should create opportunities for the player
to progressively move from:
Instruction
toward
Understanding
toward
Independent Adaptation.

-- 130 of 866 --

11.22 The Coach's Role in Learning
The coach is not simply the person who provides answers.
The coach designs the conditions in which learning can occur.
The coach may:
• Create problems.
• Manipulate constraints.
• Ask questions.
• Provide feedback.
• Observe behavior.
• Adjust difficulty.
• Encourage reflection.
• Identify when direct instruction is necessary.
The coaching objective gradually shifts from:
Controlling the player's behavior
to
Developing the player's ability to regulate their own
behavior.

11.23 Learning Capacity Progression
A useful DPF progression is:

Can absorb information with support.

11.24 Measuring Learning Capacity
Learning capacity should be assessed through behavior over
time.
Evidence may include:
Response to Feedback
Does the player modify behavior?
Rate of Adaptation
How quickly can the player adjust?
Transfer
Can learning appear in new contexts?
Reflection
Can the player explain their learning?
Problem Solving
Can the player generate solutions?
Independence
Does the player require less external instruction?
Resilience in Learning
Can the player continue experimenting after failure?
The objective is to evaluate learning behavior, not assign a
fixed intelligence label.

-- 133 of 866 --

11.25 Measuring Adaptability
Adaptability can be observed when the environment
changes.
Examples:
• New opponent.
• New role.
• New tactical problem.
• New competition level.
• Reduced time.
• Reduced space.
• Increased pressure.
The key question is:
How effectively does the player adjust when the original
solution stops working?

-- 134 of 866 --

11.26 Common Learning & Adaptability Mistakes
DPF discourages:
• Over-coaching every decision.
• Providing solutions before players explore.
• Repeating identical tasks indefinitely.
• Confusing obedience with learning.
• Measuring learning only through tests.
• Treating mistakes as purely negative.
• Ignoring transfer.
• Creating complexity without purpose.
• Developing dependence on coach feedback.
The objective is not to make players memorize more.
It is to make them learn faster, deeper, and more
independently.

-- 135 of 866 --

Chapter 12
Player Assessment & Diagnosis
12.1 Introduction
Effective player development begins with accurate
understanding.
Assessment provides evidence about the player's current
capabilities, behaviors, responses, and development
characteristics.
Diagnosis goes one step further.
It seeks to understand why the player currently performs as
they do and what underlying factors should influence the
next development decision.
Within DPF:
Assessment describes the player. Diagnosis explains the
development problem.
This distinction is fundamental.

-- 140 of 866 --

12.2 Assessment vs Diagnosis
Assessment and diagnosis are connected but not identical.
Assessment
Answers:
What can we observe?
Diagnosis
Answers:
Why is this happening?
Development Planning
Answers:
What should we do next?
Therefore:
Assessment → Diagnosis → Development Decision
The system must not jump directly from observation to
intervention.

-- 141 of 866 --

12.3 The Purpose of Assessment
Assessment exists to improve development decisions.
It should help the development team:
• Establish a baseline.
• Understand current capability.
• Identify strengths.
• Identify development needs.
• Detect changes over time.
• Understand contextual differences.
• Inform priorities.
• Evaluate interventions.
• Support progression decisions.
Assessment is therefore a decision-support mechanism, not
an end in itself.

-- 142 of 866 --

12.4 The DPF Assessment Model
Assessment operates across the seven player domains:
Technical
Execution, consistency, adaptability, functional application.
Tactical
Perception, decision-making, positioning, role understanding.
Physical
Movement, capacity, speed, strength, endurance, readiness.
Psychological
Regulation, confidence, attention, resilience, motivation.
Social
Communication, relationships, cooperation, behavior.
Learning
Feedback response, reflection, problem-solving, adaptability.
Professional
Responsibility, habits, standards, ownership, career
readiness.
These domains should be interpreted as an integrated
system.

12.5 Assessment Context
No assessment is complete without context.
Evidence should be interpreted through:
• Age.
• Maturation.
• Position.
• Role.
• Competition level.
• Game Model.
• Training environment.
• Match context.
• Previous development history.
• Current physical state.
The same behavior may have different meanings under
different conditions.
Therefore:
Context is part of the assessment, not an optional note
attached to it.

-- 144 of 866 --

12.6 Multiple Sources of Evidence
DPF does not rely on one assessment source.
Evidence may include:
Observation
Coach and development staff observation.
Competition
Match behavior and performance.
Video
Repeated behavioral patterns and contextual analysis.
Physical Data
Testing and monitoring.
Training Data
Load, exposure, response, and behavior.
Player Reflection
Self-awareness and understanding.
Staff Feedback
Input from relevant specialists.
Longitudinal History
Change across time.
The objective is triangulation.

-- 145 of 866 --

12.7 Evidence Triangulation
A single observation can be misleading.
DPF therefore seeks convergence between different evidence
sources.
For example:
Coach Observation
•
Video
•
Player Reflection
•
Performance Data
→
Stronger Development Understanding
When evidence conflicts, the conflict itself becomes
information requiring further investigation.

-- 146 of 866 --

12.8 Assessment Conditions
Assessment can occur in different environments:
Controlled
Structured testing or standardized tasks.
Semi-Controlled
Designed football problems with defined constraints.
Representative
Training situations that resemble competition.
Competitive
Actual match environments.
Each provides different information.
The more complex the behavior being assessed, the more
important contextual evidence becomes.

-- 147 of 866 --

12.9 Baseline Assessment
Before establishing a development priority, the system should
establish a meaningful baseline.
The baseline should identify:
• Current capability.
• Consistency.
• Context of success.
• Context of difficulty.
• Existing strengths.
• Development needs.
• Player perception.
• Relevant environmental factors.
The baseline becomes the reference against which future
change can be evaluated.

-- 148 of 866 --

12.10 Assessment Is Not a Ranking System
The purpose of assessment is not simply to rank players.
Two players can receive similar evaluations while requiring
completely different interventions.
Likewise, a player with lower current performance may
demonstrate:
• Strong learning capacity.
• Rapid adaptation.
• Significant improvement.
• High developmental potential.
Therefore:
Assessment should support development, not reduce
players to rankings.

12.11 Observation
Observation remains one of the most important assessment
tools.
But observation should be structured.
Instead of:
"He had a bad game."
The observer should identify:
• What happened?
• How often?
• Under what conditions?
• What was the player attempting?
• What information was available?
• What decision was made?
• What was the outcome?
• Was the behavior repeated?
This transforms opinion into usable evidence.

-- 150 of 866 --

12.12 Behavioral Evidence
DPF prioritizes observable behavior.
For example:
Instead of:
"Poor decision-maker."
Use:
"Frequently selects the forward option despite insufficient
space when pressure arrives from the blind side."
The second statement is:
• Observable.
• Contextual.
• Specific.
• Diagnosable.
• Actionable.
This is the standard DPF should seek in assessment language.

-- 151 of 866 --

12.13 Developmental Evidence vs Performance Evidence
Not every performance event represents development.
A player may perform poorly because of:
• Strong opposition.
• Tactical mismatch.
• Fatigue.
• New role.
• Environmental change.
Likewise, a strong performance may occur because:
• The opponent was weak.
• The player had unusually favorable conditions.
• The task was familiar.
Therefore, assessment should distinguish:
Performance Evidence
from
Developmental Evidence.

-- 152 of 866 --

12.14 Longitudinal Assessment
Development is change over time.
DPF therefore values repeated assessment.
The system should track:
Baseline
→ Intervention
→ Response
→ Change
→ New Baseline
This makes development measurable as a trajectory rather
than a collection of isolated snapshots.

-- 153 of 866 --

12.15 Assessment Frequency
Not every characteristic requires the same assessment
frequency.
Some indicators may require:
Continuous Observation
Others:
Weekly Review
Others:
Monthly Review
Others:
Seasonal Assessment
The frequency should reflect:
• Importance.
• Rate of change.
• Reliability of evidence.
• Player age.
• Development stage.
• Risk or performance relevance.
Assessment should be purpose-driven, not excessive.

-- 154 of 866 --

12.16 Diagnosis
Diagnosis is the bridge between evidence and development
action.
The diagnostic process asks:
What is happening?
Where does it occur?
When does it occur?
Under what conditions?
How frequently?
Why might it occur?
What factors contribute?
Is it actually the primary development problem?
Only after these questions should intervention be selected.

-- 155 of 866 --

12.17 The DPF Diagnostic Chain
The diagnostic logic is:
Behavior
↓
Pattern
↓
Context
↓
Possible Cause
↓
Evidence
↓
Diagnosis
↓
Development Priority
This prevents premature conclusions.

-- 156 of 866 --

12.18 Multi-Causal Diagnosis
Player behavior rarely has only one cause.
For example:
Poor receiving under pressure
could involve:
• Technical mechanics.
• Scanning.
• Body orientation.
• Tactical understanding.
• Confidence.
• Physical mobility.
• Environmental pressure.
Therefore:
The visible problem is not necessarily the underlying
problem.
Diagnosis must investigate the system behind the behavior.

Insufficient scanning before receiving.

D. Psychological

Insufficient mobility to adjust body position.
The correct intervention depends on the diagnosis.

12.20 Strength Diagnosis
Diagnosis should not focus only on problems.
The system should identify:
• What the player already does exceptionally well.
• Why that strength works.
• Under what conditions it works.
• How it can be expanded.
• How it can become a greater competitive advantage.
This creates:
Strength → Expansion → Specialization → Advantage

-- 159 of 866 --

12.21 Development Priority
Diagnosis may reveal many development needs.
The system must then determine which matter most.
Priority should consider:
Impact
How much does the issue affect performance?
Frequency
How consistently does it appear?
Transfer
How broadly does it affect football behavior?
Developmental Importance
How important is it for the player's pathway?
Trainability
Can meaningful improvement realistically occur?
Timing
Is this the appropriate moment to address it?

-- 160 of 866 --

12.22 Priority Matrix
A useful DPF decision model is:
High Impact + High Developmental Importance
→ Priority
High Impact + Low Trainability
→ Manage / Support
Low Impact + High Trainability
→ Secondary Development
Low Impact + Low Importance
→ Monitor
This prevents the development plan from becoming a list of
every imperfection.

-- 161 of 866 --

12.23 Assessment Language
DPF assessment language should be:
Specific
Observable
Contextual
Evidence-Based
Developmental
Non-Labeling
Avoid:
• Lazy.
• Weak mentality.
• Bad decision-maker.
• Not talented.
• Poor attitude.
Prefer behavioral descriptions.
For example:
"The player disengages from the next action after losing
possession and requires external prompting to immediately
re-enter the defensive phase."
This creates something the system can actually develop.

-- 162 of 866 --

12.24 Player Voice
The player should be an active participant in assessment.
The development team should ask:
• What do you think you're doing well?
• Where do you struggle?
• What situations feel difficult?
• What do you want to improve?
• What do you think causes the problem?
• What support would help?
Player perception should not automatically be treated as
objective truth.
But it is valuable evidence.

-- 163 of 866 --

12.28 Assessment Integrity
Assessment quality depends on:

Chapter 13

13.1 Introduction
Assessment creates understanding.
Diagnosis creates clarity.
Development planning converts that clarity into a structured
pathway for action.
The Individual Development Plan (IDP) is the mechanism
through which a player's development priorities are
translated into specific objectives, actions, responsibilities,
timelines, evidence, and review points.
Within DPF:
The IDP is not a document describing the player. It is a living
system for developing the player.

13.2 What Is an IDP?
An Individual Development Plan is a structured framework
that defines:
• What the player needs to develop.
• Why it matters.
• What successful development looks like.
• How development will occur.
• Who is responsible.
• What evidence will demonstrate progress.
• When progress will be reviewed.
The IDP connects:
Diagnosis → Development Action → Evidence → Review

13.3 Purpose of the IDP
The IDP exists to create:
Clarity
Everyone understands the development priorities.
Alignment
Coaches and support staff work toward the same objectives.
Individualization
The player's pathway reflects their specific needs.
Accountability
Responsibilities are clearly defined.
Continuity
Development remains coherent across time.
Adaptability
The plan can evolve as evidence changes.

04 — WHERE ARE WE GOING?
Desired development outcome.
05 — HOW?

06 — HOW WILL WE KNOW?

Review and adaptation.

A development intervention is a purposeful action or
environmental change designed to influence a player's
capability.
It may involve:
• Changing a training task.
• Increasing or reducing challenge.
• Manipulating space.
• Changing numerical conditions.
• Providing additional exposure.
• Altering the player's role.
• Introducing targeted practice.
• Using video.
• Providing feedback.
• Creating competitive opportunities.
• Adjusting workload.
• Introducing reflection.
The intervention must always connect to a diagnosed
development need.

The fundamental DPF sequence is:

↓

↓
Diagnosis
↓
Priority
↓
Intervention
The system should never begin with:
"What drill should we use?"
It begins with:
"What capability are we trying to change, and what is
preventing it from emerging?"
Only then should the intervention be designed.

Training is the broader environment through which players

04. Challenge
Increase the difficulty of the problem.
05. Feedback
Improve understanding and adjustment.
06. Reflection
Help the player convert experience into learning.
07. Competition
Test transfer under authentic conditions.
These levers can be combined.

be manufactured through isolated practice.

Chapter 15
Development Monitoring, Review & Progression
15.1 Introduction
Development is not validated by intention.
A player may receive an excellent assessment, a well-
designed IDP, and carefully constructed interventions, yet
meaningful development may still fail to occur.
Monitoring and review provide the evidence required to
determine whether development is progressing.
Progression then determines how the player's developmental
pathway should evolve.
Within DPF:
Monitor the change. Review the evidence. Adapt the
challenge. Progress the player.

-- 237 of 866 --

15.2 The Purpose of Monitoring
Monitoring provides continuous information about the
player's response to development.
It helps answer:
• Is the player responding?
• Is the target behavior changing?
• Is improvement consistent?
• Is the player transferring learning?
• Is the intervention appropriate?
• Is the current challenge still suitable?
Monitoring is therefore not surveillance.
It is developmental feedback.

-- 238 of 866 --

15.3 Monitoring vs Review
These concepts must remain distinct.
Monitoring
Continuous or regular observation of development.
What is changing?
Review
Structured interpretation of accumulated evidence.
What does the change mean?
Progression
Decision about what should happen next.
What level of challenge or pathway should follow?
Therefore:
Monitor → Review → Decide → Adapt

-- 239 of 866 --

15.4 The DPF Monitoring Model
Monitoring should consider five dimensions:
Behavior
What is the player actually doing?
Consistency
Can the behavior be reproduced?
Context
Does it survive different situations?
Transfer
Does it appear in competition?
Independence
Can the player produce it without constant external support?
This moves assessment beyond isolated success.

-- 240 of 866 --

15.5 Development Evidence
Evidence may come from:
• Training observation.
• Competition.
• Video.
• Performance data.
• Physical monitoring.
• Player reflection.
• Coach feedback.
• Specialist feedback.
• Longitudinal records.
The objective is not maximum data.
The objective is useful evidence for better decisions.

-- 241 of 866 --

15.6 Leading vs Lagging Evidence
DPF distinguishes between:
Leading Indicators
Early evidence that development may be occurring.
Examples:
• Improved scanning frequency.
• Better body orientation.
• Improved training behavior.
• Increased reflection.
• Better response to feedback.
Lagging Indicators
Evidence of broader performance impact.
Examples:
• Competition performance.
• Role effectiveness.
• Consistent execution.
• Increased playing contribution.
Leading indicators help the system detect change before final
performance outcomes fully appear.

15.7 Development Is Not Always Linear
Player development can include:
Acceleration
Rapid improvement.
Stabilization

Reorganization
The player changes behavior while adapting to a new level of
demand.

Context matters.

15.10 Review of the Diagnosis
An important DPF principle:
If the intervention does not work, reassess the diagnosis.
Failure to improve may mean:
• The intervention was ineffective.
• The dosage was wrong.
• The environment was inappropriate.
• The player needed more time.
• The target was poorly defined.
• The original diagnosis was incomplete.
• Another factor is limiting progress.
Therefore:
No Progress ≠ Automatically More Training
Sometimes the correct response is:
Better Diagnosis.

15.11 Review of the Intervention
The development team should evaluate:
• Was the intervention appropriate?
• Was it sufficiently challenging?
• Was there enough exposure?
• Was feedback effective?
• Was the player engaged?
• Was the environment representative?
• Did the intervention transfer?
The intervention itself becomes part of the review.
15.12 Player Review
The player's perspective is essential.
The player should increasingly be able to answer:
• What am I improving?
• What still feels difficult?
• Where do I perform best?
• What has helped?
• What has not helped?
• What challenge do I need next?
This strengthens:

15.14 Review Outcomes
Every review should result in a clear decision.
Continue
The intervention is working.
Modify
The objective remains valid, but the method changes.
Progress
The player is ready for greater challenge.
Regress
The demand should temporarily be reduced.
Reassess
The original diagnosis requires investigation.
Close
The objective has been sufficiently achieved.
Replace
A more important development priority has emerged.
This prevents reviews from becoming descriptive meetings
with no action.

15.15 Progression
Progression means increasing the player's developmental
challenge when evidence suggests readiness.
Progression may involve:
• Greater competition.
• More responsibility.
• Stronger opposition.
• Reduced time.
• Reduced space.
• Greater tactical complexity.
• Increased physical demand.
• Greater role responsibility.
• Increased independence.
Progression should be based on readiness, not simply age.

-- 250 of 866 --

15.16 Readiness vs Age
Chronological age can provide context.
It should not be the sole determinant of progression.
Readiness may depend on:
• Current capability.
• Consistency.
• Adaptability.
• Physical development.
• Psychological readiness.
• Learning capacity.
• Role requirements.
• Competition demands.
• Professional behavior.
Therefore:
Age describes where the player is in time. Readiness
describes what the player can handle next.

-- 251 of 866 --

Progression should follow:

↓
Consistency
↓

↓

↓

↓

not just the physical dimension.

Progression can occur in two ways.
Vertical Progression
Moving toward a higher level of competition or responsibility.
Example:
Academy → Reserve → First Team.
Horizontal Progression
Expanding capability within the same level.
Example:
One role → Additional role capability.
or:
Basic execution → More adaptable execution.
Both forms contribute to development.

Pressure

Opposition

Responsibility

Uncertainty

Consequence

Independence

Progression should target the specific developmental
constraint.

A setback should trigger analysis rather than panic.
Possible responses:
Stabilize
Provide support.
↓
Understand
Identify what changed.
↓

Modify development conditions.
↓
Rebuild
Restore capability.
↓

15.24 Development Plateau
A plateau can occur when:
• The current challenge is too easy.
• The intervention has reached its limits.
• The player requires a new context.
• A hidden constraint exists.
• The player has reached a temporary adaptation ceiling.
The response should not automatically be:
Do more.
It may instead be:
Change the problem.
15.25 Development Acceleration
Some players may demonstrate rapid adaptation.
The system should be able to respond by:
• Increasing challenge.
• Providing stronger competition.
• Expanding responsibility.
• Introducing more complex problems.
• Increasing independence.
This prevents highly responsive players from being held at an
inappropriate developmental level simply because the schedule says
otherwise.

Players do not progress at identical rates.
Therefore:

• Different maturation.
• Different learning capacity.
• Different experience.
• Different physical development.
• Different psychological development.
• Different environments.
This is one of the foundations of genuine individualization.

Chapter 16
Elite Player Pathway
16.1 Introduction
Player development is not a collection of isolated training
cycles.
It is a progressive pathway through which players encounter
increasingly demanding environments, responsibilities, and
standards.
The Elite Player Pathway defines how DPF moves a player
from developmental participation toward higher levels of
football performance and responsibility.
The pathway is not designed to accelerate every player at the
same speed.
It is designed to identify the right next environment for each
player's current capability, readiness, and developmental
trajectory.
The pathway should not ask how quickly a player can move
upward. It should ask what environment will develop the
player best next.

16.2 What Is the Elite Player Pathway?
The Elite Player Pathway is the structured progression
through which a player moves across increasingly demanding
stages of development.
It integrates:
• Capability.
• Readiness.
• Competition.
• Role.
• Learning capacity.
• Physical development.
• Psychological development.
• Professional behavior.
• Player ownership.
The pathway connects developmental progression with
environmental progression.

-- 269 of 866 --

16.3 Development vs Pathway
These concepts must remain distinct.
Player Development
The change in the player's capability.
Player Pathway
The sequence of environments through which that capability
is developed and tested.
Therefore:
Development changes the player.
The pathway changes the demands placed on the player.
Both must progress together.

-- 270 of 866 --

16.4 The DPF Elite Pathway Model
A simplified pathway may progress through:
Stage 01
Foundation
Building fundamental football and learning capabilities.
Stage 02
Development
Increasing technical, tactical, physical, psychological, and
social capability.
Stage 03
Performance
Expressing capability consistently in competitive
environments.
Stage 04
Elite Development
Handling greater complexity, pressure, responsibility, and
competition.
Stage 05
Professional Preparation
Preparing for the demands of senior football.

Stage 06
Professional Transition
Entering and adapting to professional football.
The exact age boundaries should remain flexible.
16.5 Age Is a Reference, Not a Definition
Age-group structures provide organization.
They should not become the definition of development.
Two players of the same age may differ significantly in:
• Maturation.
• Experience.
• Physical capability.
• Tactical understanding.
• Learning capacity.
• Psychological readiness.
• Competition readiness.
Therefore:
Age organizes the pathway. Readiness determines
progression.

Readiness represents the player's capacity to handle the
demands of the next environment.
It includes:

Psychological Readiness
Can the player manage the increased pressure?
Learning Capacity
Can the player adapt to new demands?
Social & Professional Readiness
Can the player function responsibly within the environment?
Readiness is therefore multidimensional.

Chapter 17
Transition to Professional Football
17.1 Introduction
Reaching professional football is not the end of player
development.
It is the beginning of a new developmental environment with
greater demands, uncertainty, responsibility, and competition.
The transition from academy or elite development football into
professional football requires more than football ability.
The player must be prepared to manage:
• Increased competition.
• Higher physical demands.
• Greater tactical complexity.
• Professional expectations.
• Reduced certainty.
• Greater independence.
• Career decisions.
• New relationships.
• Public and commercial pressures.
Within DPF:
Professional transition is not an event. It is a managed
developmental process.

-- 299 of 866 --

17.2 What Is Professional Transition?
Professional transition is the process through which a player
moves from a developmental environment into the demands
of senior professional football.
It includes three dimensions:
Entry
Getting access to the professional environment.
Integration
Learning to function effectively within it.
Sustainability
Maintaining development and performance after entry.
A player has not completed the transition simply because
they sign a professional contract.

-- 300 of 866 --

17.3 Contract vs Transition
These must remain separate.
Contract
A formal professional agreement.
Transition
The player's ability to successfully function within
professional football.
Therefore:
Contract ≠ Professional Readiness
and:
Professional Entry ≠ Professional Integration
The real objective is sustainable professional capability.

-- 301 of 866 --

The transition can be represented through five stages:
01
Preparation
Build readiness before entry.
02
Entry
Enter the professional environment.
03
Integration
Adapt to the new demands.
04
Establishment
Become increasingly capable and reliable.
05
Sustainability
Continue developing and performing over time.

17.5 Preparation
Preparation should begin before the player enters
professional football.
The player should progressively understand:
• Training expectations.
• Competition demands.
• Professional routines.
• Recovery responsibilities.
• Tactical expectations.
• Communication standards.
• Personal responsibility.
• Career realities.

17.6 Professional Readiness
Professional readiness is multidimensional.
Football Readiness
Can the player meet the technical and tactical requirements?
Physical Readiness
Can the player tolerate professional demands?
Psychological Readiness
Can the player manage uncertainty and pressure?
Learning Readiness
Can the player adapt rapidly?
Social Readiness
Can the player function within a professional environment?
Professional Readiness
Can the player manage responsibilities independently?
The player does not need to be perfect in every dimension.
They need sufficient readiness to benefit from the
environment.

Entry may occur through:
• First-team integration.
• Professional contract.
• Senior training.
• Competitive debut.
• Reserve or B-team football.
• Loan placement.
• Other structured senior environments.
The pathway can therefore have multiple entry routes.
There is no single definition of the professional transition
experience.

The first professional environment can be significantly
different from academy football.
Players may encounter:
• Faster decision-making.
• Greater physical intensity.
• Experienced opponents.
• Higher tactical demands.
• Stronger competition for selection.
• Less tolerance for repeated errors.
• Greater performance consequences.
The player must adapt without losing their developmental
identity.

• Role responsibilities.
• Training standards.
• Communication patterns.
• Professional routines.
• Recovery requirements.
• Organizational culture.

Chapter 19
Player Welfare, Protection & Wellbeing
19.1 Introduction
Player development cannot be separated from player
welfare.
A player may possess significant football potential while
simultaneously experiencing circumstances that negatively
affect their ability to learn, perform, develop, or remain
within the game.
DPF therefore considers welfare and wellbeing fundamental
conditions for sustainable development.
Player welfare includes the systems, relationships,
environments, and practices that support the player's:
• Safety.
• Dignity.
• Physical wellbeing.
• Psychological wellbeing.
• Social wellbeing.
• Developmental continuity.
• Protection from harm.
• Ability to seek support.
Protect the person. Develop the player. Sustain the career.

-- 366 of 866 --

19.2 Welfare vs Wellbeing vs Protection
These concepts are connected but different.
Welfare
The broader conditions that support the player's health,
safety, development, and quality of life.
Wellbeing
The player's ongoing physical, psychological, emotional, and
social state.
Protection
The systems and responsibilities designed to prevent,
identify, and respond to harm.
Together:
Welfare + Wellbeing + Protection
→ Safe Development Environment

Every development decision should ultimately consider:

• Exploitation.
• Neglect.
• Unsafe pressure.
• Humiliation.
• Abuse.
• Unreasonable workload.
• Loss of dignity.
The objective is:
Challenge without harm.

19.15 Recognizing Warning Signs
Development staff should be attentive to meaningful changes
in behavior.
Potential warning signs may include:
• Sudden withdrawal.
• Unusual fear.
• Significant behavioral changes.
• Repeated unexplained absences.
• Declining wellbeing.
• Changes in relationships.
• Unusual distress.
• Reluctance to interact with particular individuals.
No single sign automatically establishes what has happened.
The appropriate response is:

safeguarding procedures → Escalate when required

• Avoid judgment.
• Avoid promising absolute confidentiality.

• Escalate appropriately.
The objective is not for every coach to investigate.

Chapter 20

20.1 Introduction
A safe development environment cannot depend solely on
good intentions.
Player protection requires clear standards, defined
responsibilities, reporting pathways, professional boundaries,
risk management, and organizational accountability.
Within DPF, safeguarding is therefore understood as an
institutional responsibility, not an individual preference.
A safe environment is designed, governed, monitored, and
continuously improved.

20.2 What Is Safe Sport?
Safe Sport refers to the conditions required for players to
participate, develop, and compete without being exposed to
preventable harm, abuse, exploitation, discrimination, or
inappropriate conduct.
It includes:
• Safe environments.
• Appropriate behavior.
• Professional boundaries.
• Player protection.
• Fair treatment.
• Risk management.
• Reporting mechanisms.
• Organizational accountability.

• Training.
• Competition.
• Travel.
• Accommodation.
• Medical environments.
• Digital communication.
• Development activities.
• Transitions.

organizational structure, but the DPF principle remains
consistent:
Responsibility increases with the organization's influence
over the player's environment.

• Appropriate accommodation standards.
• Safe communication channels.

• Appropriate reporting channel.
• External authority where required.

Support

Players must be able to raise concerns without fear that

• Playing time.
• Development.
• Relationships.
• Contracts.

• Supervision.
• Consent processes where applicable.

• Accommodation.
• Digital communication.
• Parent / guardian communication.
• Education.
• Reporting access.

Chapter 21
Health, Load, Recovery & Availability
21.1 Introduction
A player's ability to develop depends partly on their ability to
train, recover, compete, and remain available.
Development cannot be sustained when the player is
repeatedly exposed to demands that exceed their ability to
adapt.
DPF therefore treats health, load, recovery, and availability as
interconnected components of the player's developmental
environment.
The objective is not:
Maximum Load
It is:
Optimal Adaptation + Sustainable Availability
Evidence from IOC consensus work supports individualized
monitoring of training and competition load, wellbeing,
illness, recovery, and psychological stress rather than treating
workload as a single universal number.

-- 439 of 866 --

21.2 The DPF Principle
The central relationship is:
Load
↓
Response
↓
Recovery
↓
Adaptation
↓
Availability
↓
Performance & Development
If recovery is insufficient, adaptation may be compromised.
If load is consistently inappropriate, injury, illness,
maladaptation, or performance decline may occur.

-- 440 of 866 --

21.3 What Is Load?
Load is the total demand placed on the player.
It can include:
External Load
What the player does.
• Distance.
• High-speed running.
• Accelerations.
• Decelerations.
• Training duration.
• Match exposure.
• Number of sessions.
Internal Load
How the player responds.
• Perceived exertion.
• Physiological response.
• Fatigue.
• Wellbeing.
• Psychological stress.

-- 441 of 866 --

Non-Sport Load
Development does not happen in a vacuum.
The player may also experience:
• Education.
• Travel.
• Family demands.
• Social stress.
• Career uncertainty.
• Sleep disruption.
The total stress experienced by the player matters.

21.4 Load Is Individual
Two players can complete the same session while
experiencing very different demands.
Therefore:
Same Activity ≠ Same Load
Load management must consider:
• Player history.
• Current capacity.
• Training age.
• Physical development.
• Competition exposure.
• Recovery.
• Psychological state.
• Current health.
This is particularly important in youth development, where
growth and maturation can alter how players respond to
training and competition.

-- 443 of 866 --

21.5 Load Is Not the Enemy
A common mistake is to treat load as inherently harmful.
Load is necessary for adaptation.
The problem is not:
Load
The problem is:
Inappropriate Load
Development requires enough stimulus to create adaptation
while allowing sufficient recovery.
21.6 The Load–Recovery Relationship
A useful DPF model:
Stimulus
→ Fatigue
→ Recovery
→ Adaptation
→ Increased Capacity
→ New Stimulus
This creates progressive development.
If recovery repeatedly fails:

→ Reduced Adaptation

The system must therefore manage both sides of the

21.7 Recovery
Recovery is not simply "doing nothing."
It may involve:
• Sleep.
• Nutrition.
• Hydration.
• Appropriate rest.
• Active recovery.
• Physical recovery strategies.
• Psychological recovery.
• Reduced training demand.
• Appropriate medical support.
IOC consensus guidance emphasizes individualized recovery
planning, including sleep, nutrition, hydration, rest, and
psychological recovery.

21.8 Sleep
Sleep is a major component of recovery and development.
It influences:
• Physical recovery.
• Learning.
• Cognitive function.
• Emotional regulation.
• Performance.
• General wellbeing.
This becomes particularly important for youth athletes,
whose development and irregular schedules can make
adequate sleep more difficult.
The DPF principle is therefore:
Protect recovery capacity, not simply schedule more
training.

21.9 Nutrition & Hydration
Nutrition and hydration support:
• Training adaptation.
• Recovery.
• Energy availability.
• Performance.
• Growth.
• General health.
For younger players, nutritional guidance must account for
normal growth and maturation in addition to sporting
demands.
Specific nutritional prescriptions belong with appropriately
qualified professionals.

Psychological stress can influence:
• Recovery.
• Sleep.
• Motivation.
• Concentration.
• Immune function.
• Training response.
Therefore:
Training Load + Competition Load + Life Stress
should be considered when interpreting player response.

• Time-zone changes.

• Reduced recovery time.

Availability means the player's ability to participate appropriately in
training and competition.

participation or graduated exposure.

Sustainable availability creates developmental continuity.

• Environment.
• Education.

• Wellbeing.
• Recovery.
• Performance changes.
• Relevant medical indicators.

psychological conditions required for sustainable
development.
The objective is not to eliminate fatigue, challenge, or load.
It is to manage them intelligently.
The DPF approach therefore seeks:
Appropriate Load
→ Adequate Recovery
→ Adaptation
→ Availability
→ Development
→ Performance
→ Longevity
"The best development system does not keep players
available for today at the expense of keeping them
developing tomorrow."

Chapter 22
Psychological Safety, Belonging & Emotional Support
22.1 Introduction
A player cannot be reduced to performance outputs.
Football development takes place within an emotional,
psychological, and social environment that influences how
players learn, respond to pressure, interact with others, and
sustain their development.
The IOC has emphasized that athlete mental health is
inseparable from physical health and that effective support
requires attention not only to the individual athlete, but also
to the environment in which they train and compete.
Within DPF:
Create an environment where the player can compete
seriously, fail safely, ask for help, belong meaningfully, and
continue developing.

-- 476 of 866 --

22.2 Psychological Safety
Psychological safety means that players can participate,
communicate, learn, and raise concerns without
unreasonable fear of humiliation, retaliation, or exclusion.
It does not mean:
• No criticism.
• No accountability.
• No competition.
• No consequences.
• No performance standards.
It means:
High standards without psychological harm.

-- 477 of 866 --

unreasonable fear of humiliation, retaliation, or exclusion.
It does not mean:

It means:
High standards without psychological harm.

-- 477 of 866 --

22.3 Psychological Safety vs Comfort
These concepts must not be confused.
Comfort
The player avoids difficult experiences.
Psychological Safety
The player can face difficult experiences without feeling that their
dignity or belonging is constantly threatened.
Development requires challenge.
Psychological safety allows the player to engage with challenge
productively.
22.4 Why It Matters to Development
A player who fears mistakes may:
• Avoid difficult decisions.
• Hide uncertainty.
• Stop asking questions.
• Become overly risk-averse.
• Conceal problems.
• Depend excessively on external instruction.
A psychologically safer environment can support:
Questioning → Experimentation → Feedback → Learning →
Adaptation
This makes psychological safety a developmental variable, not merely
a welfare concept.

-- 478 of 866 --

22.5 The Error Environment
Mistakes are inevitable in football.
The developmental question is:
What happens after the mistake?
A productive environment creates:
Mistake → Information → Feedback → Adjustment →
Reattempt
A destructive environment can create:
Mistake → Fear → Concealment → Avoidance → Reduced
Learning
The objective is not to celebrate every error.
It is to extract learning from error without humiliating the
player.

-- 479 of 866 --

22.6 Feedback Environment
Feedback should improve the player's understanding.
Effective feedback should be:
• Specific.
• Relevant.
• Timely.
• Respectful.
• Actionable.
• Proportionate.
The player should understand:
What happened?
Why did it matter?
What can I do differently?
Feedback should challenge behavior, not attack identity.

-- 480 of 866 --

22.7 Performance Criticism vs Personal Attack
A healthy development environment distinguishes:
"Your body position limited your next action."
from:
"You're useless."
The first evaluates behavior.
The second attacks identity.
DPF requires high standards without degrading the individual.

-- 481 of 866 --

22.8 Belonging
Belonging means the player experiences genuine
membership within the environment.
It involves:
• Inclusion.
• Respect.
• Recognition.
• Relationships.
• Participation.
• Shared identity.
A player can be highly talented and still feel disconnected.
Development requires more than technical inclusion.
It requires social inclusion.

-- 482 of 866 --

22.9 Belonging and Performance
Belonging can influence:
Connection
→ Engagement
→ Participation
→ Learning
→ Performance
Conversely, persistent exclusion may contribute to:
Isolation
→ Reduced engagement
→ Reduced learning
→ Reduced development
The development environment should therefore actively
create meaningful connection.

-- 483 of 866 --

22.10 Team Integration
Integration is not simply putting a player inside the squad.
It involves helping the player understand:
• Team norms.
• Communication.
• Expectations.
• Relationships.
• Role.
• Culture.
• Standards.
This is particularly important during transitions between age
groups and into senior football.

22.11 The New Player
New players may experience:
• Uncertainty.
• Social isolation.
• Fear of judgment.
• Language barriers.
• Cultural differences.
• Pressure to prove themselves.
A structured integration process can reduce unnecessary
friction.
The goal is:
Belonging without removing the challenge of earning trust
through performance and behavior.

-- 485 of 866 --

22.12 Emotional Support
Players may experience emotional strain through:
• Selection.
• Non-selection.
• Injury.
• Transfers.
• Contract uncertainty.
• Performance fluctuations.
• Family circumstances.
• Career transitions.
Not every emotional difficulty is a clinical mental health
condition.
But every meaningful concern deserves appropriate
attention.

-- 486 of 866 --

22.13 Support vs Treatment
This distinction is important.
Support
Listening, connection, education, practical assistance, and
appropriate referral.
Treatment
Clinical intervention delivered by appropriately qualified
professionals.
Coaches and development staff should know where their role
ends.
Support does not mean pretending to be a clinician.
The IOC recommends an integrated approach involving
appropriate professional care and environmental support for
athlete mental health.

-- 487 of 866 --

22.14 Help-Seeking
A strong environment makes asking for help normal.
The player should know:
• Who to approach.
• How to approach them.
• What happens next.
• What confidentiality means.
• When information may need to be escalated.
The objective is to make help-seeking part of professional
self-care rather than a sign of weakness.

-- 488 of 866 --

22.15 The DPF Help-Seeking Pathway

↓
Speak
↓
Listen
↓
Assess
↓
Support / Refer
↓
Follow Up
This pathway complements the safeguarding response system
from Chapter 20.

-- 489 of 866 --

22.16 Emotional Regulation
Players progressively need to manage:
• Frustration.
• Disappointment.
• Pressure.
• Anger.
• Anxiety.
• Excitement.
• Failure.
• Uncertainty.
The objective is not emotional suppression.
It is:
Recognize → Understand → Regulate → Respond
This supports performance and personal development.

-- 490 of 866 --

22.17 Resilience
DPF does not define resilience as:
“Just deal with it.”
Resilience is the capacity to adapt to difficulty while using
appropriate resources and support.
It involves:
• Recovery.
• Learning.
• Perspective.
• Adaptation.
• Support.
• Re-engagement.
Strong players are not players who never struggle.
They are players who can respond constructively to struggle.

-- 491 of 866 --

22.18 Confidence
Confidence should not depend entirely on recent
performance.
A healthier developmental model builds confidence through:
Capability
•
Preparation
•
Experience
•
Support
•
Self-awareness
Confidence then becomes more stable than:
"I played well today, therefore I am good."

22.19 Identity
Young players especially may begin to define themselves
almost entirely through football.
This can create vulnerability when:
• They are injured.
• They are not selected.
• Their development slows.
• They leave a club.
• Their career changes.
A broader identity can provide psychological stability.
Football can be:
A major part of identity
without becoming:
The entirety of identity.

-- 493 of 866 --

22.20 Dual Identity
Players can develop:
Football Identity
•
Human Identity
The second may include:
• Education.
• Family.
• Friends.
• Interests.
• Values.
• Community.
• Future ambitions.
This does not weaken commitment to football.
It can help create greater psychological stability across the
career.

-- 494 of 866 --

22.21 Pressure
Pressure is not inherently harmful.
Some pressure can stimulate:
• Focus.
• Preparation.
• Motivation.
• Performance.
The problem emerges when pressure becomes:
• Chronic.
• Unmanageable.
• Personal.
• Threatening.
• Unsupported.
Therefore:
Challenge + Support
is more productive than:
Pressure + Fear

-- 495 of 866 --

22.22 Selection Pressure
Selection creates uncertainty.
Players may constantly wonder:
"Am I playing?"
"Am I progressing?"
"Will I get a contract?"
"Am I still valued?"
The development environment should provide clarity around:
• Current status.
• Expectations.
• Development priorities.
• Review process.
Certainty about the process can reduce unnecessary
uncertainty about the person.

-- 496 of 866 --

22.23 Non-Selection
Non-selection should be handled as a developmental event.
The player should receive:
Explanation
•
Feedback
•
Development Direction
•
Next Opportunity
The objective is not to remove disappointment.
It is to prevent disappointment from becoming identity
damage.

-- 497 of 866 --

22.24 Injury and Psychological Wellbeing
Injury can disrupt:
• Routine.
• Team connection.
• Identity.
• Confidence.
• Career expectations.
The player should remain socially and developmentally
connected wherever appropriate.
This connects directly to Chapter 21's health and availability
architecture.
Mental health and physical health should not be treated as
separate worlds. The IOC consensus specifically notes their
interaction, including links between mental health difficulties,
injury risk, and recovery.

-- 498 of 866 --

22.25 Transition Stress
Transitions can create psychological pressure.
Examples:
Academy → First Team
Club → New Club
Youth → Senior Football
Home Country → Foreign Country
Playing → Retirement
Each transition introduces:
New Environment + New Expectations + New Uncertainty
The system should provide preparation and support.

22.26 Cultural Adaptation
International players may encounter:
• Language differences.
• Cultural norms.
• Food differences.
• Religious or social practices.
• Family separation.
• Different football cultures.
Integration should therefore consider the whole person.
Cultural adaptation is not about forcing players to abandon
identity.
It is about helping them function effectively within the new
environment.
22.27 Leadership & Emotional Climate
Senior players influence the emotional environment.
Leadership can create:
Safety + Standards + Belonging
or:
Fear + Isolation + Silence
Therefore, leadership development should include awareness
of the emotional consequences of behavior.

-- 500 of 866 --

22.28 Coach Behavior
Coaches are one of the most important interpersonal
interfaces in football.
They influence:
• Psychological climate.
• Feedback.
• Trust.
• Belonging.
• Help-seeking.
• Player confidence.
The IOC has specifically highlighted coaches' role in creating
environments that reduce stigma around mental-health help-
seeking and support athlete wellbeing.
The coach does not need to become a therapist.
But the coach should know:
How to notice. How to communicate. How to refer.

-- 501 of 866 --

22.29 The Player Voice
Player voice should be built into the development system.
Methods may include:
• Development conversations.
• Welfare check-ins.
• Anonymous feedback.
• Player councils.
• Exit interviews.
• Structured surveys.
• One-to-one conversations.
The objective is to understand:
What the system looks like from inside the player's
experience.

-- 502 of 866 --

22.30 Psychological Safety Monitoring
Monitoring should not become invasive psychological
surveillance.
Useful signals may include:
• Engagement.
• Withdrawal.
• Sudden behavioral changes.
• Player-reported wellbeing.
• Help-seeking.
• Team integration.
• Confidence.
• Motivation.
Where clinical assessment is required, appropriately qualified
professionals should lead it. The IOC's SMHAT-1 was
specifically developed for trained health professionals rather
than as a coach-administered diagnostic tool.

-- 503 of 866 --

The player may be supported by:

↓
Coach
Player Development
Medical
Psychology / Mental Health
Family
Safeguarding
Education
Appropriate Professional Support
The network should remain coordinated without turning the
player into the passive center of a giant committee.

-- 504 of 866 --

22.33 The DPF Psychological Safety Model
The system can be represented through five pillars:
TRUST
Players can communicate.
BELONGING
Players feel included.
VOICE
Players can influence and raise concerns.
SUPPORT
Players can access appropriate help.
RESILIENCE
Players learn to respond constructively to challenge.
Together:
Trust + Belonging + Voice + Support + Resilience
→ Psychologically Safe Development Environment

-- 506 of 866 --

22.34 Common Failures
DPF avoids:
"Be Tough"
Confusing resilience with emotional suppression.
Fear-Based Coaching
Using humiliation as motivation.
False Positivity
Pretending every player is fine.
Clinical Overreach
Coaches attempting to diagnose mental health conditions.
No Referral Pathway
Asking players to speak up without providing support.
Performance-Only Identity
Treating the player as their statistics.
Social Exclusion
Ignoring belonging during transitions.
Silent Suffering
Assuming quiet players are necessarily okay.
Over-Monitoring
Turning wellbeing into constant surveillance.

-- 507 of 866 --

The complete system becomes:
TRUST
↓
VOICE
↓
BELONGING
↓
SUPPORT
↓
RESILIENCE
↓
LEARNING
↓
PERFORMANCE
↓
SUSTAINABILITY
This connects psychological wellbeing directly to the wider
DPF development system.

-- 508 of 866 --

Chapter Summary
Psychological safety does not lower standards.
It creates the conditions in which players can engage
seriously with high standards.
A strong DPF environment allows players to:
• Make mistakes.
• Receive difficult feedback.
• Ask for help.
• Recover from setbacks.
• Belong to the group.
• Develop confidence.
• Build resilience.
• Maintain identity beyond performance.
Mental health support should be accessible and integrated
into athlete care, while clinical assessment and treatment
remain the responsibility of appropriately qualified
professionals.
"The strongest development environment is not the one
where players never struggle. It is the one where players do
not have to struggle alone."

Chapter 23
Player Development Governance
23.1 Introduction
A Player Development system cannot depend on individual
excellence alone.
Even highly capable coaches and development professionals
can produce inconsistent outcomes when:
• Responsibilities are unclear.
• Information is fragmented.
• Decisions are disconnected.
• Development priorities conflict.
• Accountability is weak.
• Player interests are not represented.
• Staff change disrupts continuity.
Player Development therefore requires a governance
structure that coordinates people, information, decisions,
and accountability around the player's long-term
development.
Within DPF:
Governance creates the conditions in which Player
Development can operate consistently, coherently, and
responsibly.

23.2 What Is Player Development Governance?
Player Development Governance is the system through which
an organization:
• Defines ownership.
• Allocates responsibility.
• Coordinates expertise.
• Establishes decision rights.
• Manages development information.
• Resolves conflicts.
• Protects player interests.
• Reviews development outcomes.
• Maintains accountability.
It answers five fundamental questions:
Who owns development?
Who contributes?
Who decides?
Who is accountable?
How do we know the system is working?

-- 512 of 866 --

23.3 Governance Is Not Management
These concepts should remain distinct.
Governance
Defines:
Direction + Authority + Accountability + Decision Rights
Management
Coordinates:
People + Processes + Resources + Execution
Coaching
Directly influences:
Training + Learning + Performance
Player Development requires all three.

-- 513 of 866 --

23.4 The DPF Governance Principle
The player remains the center of the system.
The organizational structure exists to serve development.
Therefore:
Governance
↓
Coordination
↓
Development Environment
↓
Player
The structure should never become more important than the
player it exists to develop.

-- 514 of 866 --

23.5 One Player, One Development System
A player may interact with:
• Coach.
• Academy Director.
• Player Development Staff.
• Performance Staff.
• Medical Team.
• Psychology.
• Analysis.
• Education.
• Family.
• Representative.
But the player should not experience these as disconnected
systems.
The objective is:
Many specialists. One development logic.

-- 515 of 866 --

23.6 Clear Ownership
One of the most important governance principles is:
Shared responsibility does not mean shared ownership.
Many professionals can contribute to development.
But there should be clear ownership of:
• The player's development process.
• The IDP.
• Development reviews.
• Major pathway decisions.
• Communication.
Without clear ownership, responsibility becomes diffused.

-- 516 of 866 --

23.7 Development Owner
The Development Owner is the person or function
responsible for coordinating the player's overall development
process.
This does not mean they personally control every aspect.
Instead, they ensure that:
• Assessment is connected.
• Priorities are clear.
• Interventions are coordinated.
• Evidence is reviewed.
• Decisions are documented.
• Relevant specialists communicate.
• The player remains informed.
The exact title may vary between organizations.
The function must exist.

-- 517 of 866 --

Different decisions require different decision owners.
For example:

Qualified Medical Professional
Physical Programming
Performance / Physical Staff
Psychological Intervention

Development Priority
Player Development + Relevant Football Staff
Pathway Decision
Appropriate Technical / Development Leadership
The objective is not to create bureaucracy.
It is to ensure that:
The right decision is made by the right authority using the
right evidence.

Football behavior

Physical response

Health

Psychological wellbeing

23.11 The Player as a Participant
The player is not merely the subject of development
decisions.
They should progressively participate in:
• Goal setting.
• Review.
• Feedback.
• Development planning.
• Pathway conversations.
• Career decisions.
As players mature:
Participation

-- 521 of 866 --

23.12 The Player Voice in Governance
Player voice provides information that organizational
structures cannot generate by themselves.
It can reveal:
• Development barriers.
• Cultural problems.
• Communication failures.
• Welfare concerns.
• Misunderstood expectations.
• Environmental strengths.
Therefore:
A system that never listens to players is governing with
incomplete information.

-- 522 of 866 --

23.13 Development Meetings
Development meetings should have a clear purpose.
A useful structure is:
Before
Evidence + current priorities.
During
Interpretation + discussion + player voice.
Decision
Clear outcome.
After
Actions + ownership + timeline.
The meeting should end with:
Who does what next?

-- 523 of 866 --

23.14 Information Governance
Player Development generates significant information.
Examples include:
• Assessments.
• IDPs.
• Training observations.
• Match data.
• Physical data.
• Medical information.
• Psychological information.
• Welfare information.
• Development reviews.
The system must distinguish between:
Useful Information
and
Information That Should Not Be Widely Shared.

Especially sensitive information requires appropriate:
• Privacy.
• Security.
• Access control.
• Professional boundaries.
• Legal compliance.
The objective is:
Relevant information to the right person at the right time.

23.16 Development Continuity
Governance protects continuity when:
• Coaches change.
• Directors change.
• Players change teams.
• Players change age groups.
• Staff leave.
• Organizational structures evolve.
The system should preserve the development logic, not simply
the documents.
23.17 Handover Governance
A player transition should include a structured handover.
The receiving environment should understand:
• Current capability.
• Development priorities.
• Current interventions.
• Relevant context.
• Progression status.
• Important support considerations.
The handover should be:
Structured + Relevant + Secure + Actionable

-- 526 of 866 --

23.18 Conflict Resolution
Development decisions may conflict.
For example:
Coach
may prioritize immediate team performance.
while:
Player Development
may prioritize long-term development.
or:
Performance Staff
may recommend reduced exposure.
while:
Competition Staff
want the player available.
Governance must provide a mechanism to resolve such
conflicts.

-- 527 of 866 --

23.19 The DPF Conflict Principle
Conflict is not necessarily a failure.
Unmanaged conflict is.
The organization should ask:
What is the evidence?
What is the player's long-term interest?
What is the immediate requirement?
Who has decision authority?
What are the risks?
Then make the decision transparently.

-- 528 of 866 --

23.20 Short-Term vs Long-Term
Football organizations naturally face short-term pressures.
Player Development requires long-term thinking.
The governance system should distinguish:
Performance Priority
What helps the team now?
Development Priority
What helps the player progress?
Welfare Priority
What protects the player?
Organizational Priority
What serves the institution responsibly?
Strong governance seeks alignment rather than allowing one
priority to dominate automatically.

-- 529 of 866 --

Evidence
•

•
Risk

23.22 Accountability
Every major development process should have accountable
ownership.
Accountability includes:
• Who made the decision?
• What evidence was used?
• What was the intended outcome?
• When will it be reviewed?
• What happens if the outcome is different?
This does not mean blaming individuals.
It means making the system traceable.

sufficiently to preserve:
• Context.

• Decision.
• Rationale.
• Actions.
• Review date.
Documentation should support continuity, not create
unnecessary bureaucracy.

23.24 Governance Rhythm
Player Development governance should operate through
different time horizons.
Daily
Training + immediate player needs.
Weekly
Development observation + intervention coordination.
Monthly
Progress review + IDP adjustments.
Quarterly
Pathway and broader development review.
Annual
System review + pathway planning + strategic evaluation.
The exact cadence may vary.
The principle is:
Governance must have rhythm.

-- 533 of 866 --

23.25 Development Review Board
Organizations may establish a structured Development
Review Board involving relevant leaders and specialists.
Its role may include:
• Reviewing priority players.
• Evaluating progression.
• Resolving cross-functional issues.
• Reviewing pathway decisions.
• Identifying systemic barriers.
It should not become a committee that tries to micromanage
every player.

-- 534 of 866 --

23.26 Escalation
Some issues require escalation.
Examples:
• Serious welfare concerns.
• Safeguarding concerns.
• Significant health issues.
• Major pathway decisions.
• Persistent development stagnation.
• Organizational conflicts.
The escalation pathway should be:
Clear
Known
Proportionate
Timely

-- 535 of 866 --

23.27 Governance and Player Protection
Governance provides an additional layer of protection.
When decision-making is transparent and accountable, it
becomes harder for:
• Conflicts of interest.
• Personal preferences.
• Favoritism.
• Commercial pressure.
• Individual bias
to dominate player development decisions.
Governance therefore supports the principles established in
Chapters 19–22.

-- 536 of 866 --

23.28 The Role of Leadership
Leadership should establish:
• Development philosophy.
• Standards.
